speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
that Bill C-170, to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children, be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the last several weeks of compressed debate on this legislation the argument I have heard perhaps most frequently is that the family income security plan legislation is detrimental to the middle income group. This is hardly astonishing for, as I indicated in an earlier debate, the argument does have its political appeal, at least initially. I firmly believe, however, that such political appeal is tenuous and of short-term duration. It is difficult to reconcile the constant and differing demands by the opposition. On the one hand, they demand an increasing redistribution of income and, on the other hand, the same members of the opposition simultaneously espouse the cause of lowering the tax burden on our middle income groups. The facetious attempts on the part of the opposition to palm off this political sleight of hand will, I fear, damage greatly its credibility with Canadians in the long run. In other words, how can the opposition call for greater expenditures than the government is now making, yet accuse the government at the same time of placing too heavy a tax burden on the middle income groups.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: That is a matter of interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Therefore I have become increasingly convinced that such an approach is based on a cynical and disdainful regard for the intelligence of the majority of Canadians.
Needless to say, some in the opposition have advocated that the rich and the corporations should be taxed more. Of course they should be. If we are to undertake these additional financial obligations, it will be absolutely mandatory that we do so. It will be mandatory not just for the sake of the revenue which would be provided but also for the simple reason that the affluent of this country must accept their full obligation to our society generally.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Say that to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
As it stands, the government is already making a heavy investment in income security. At present, roughly $4 billion is committed to just three programs. Old age security and the guaranteed income supplement for the aged, with the increases voted by Parliament in December, 1970, and again last month, will represent expenditures of about $2.5 billion. The legislation now before the House represents an additional $800 million, and perhaps more. In addition, the federal 50 per cent share of provincial allotments for social assistance and social support and rehabilitation services means another $800 million in expenditures. With these facts in the background I should like to deal with some of the proposals I have heard opposition members raise.
Some in the opposition say that what we are proposing is not enough. For example, when the Family Income Security Plan legislation was last before the House some in the opposition talked about increasing the benefits over and above those recommended in the present bill as well as making those increased benefits universal. Just to make the benefits universal at the present levels, let alone provide increases, would require an additional $700 million over and above the $800 million that is now recommended.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The minister forgets that these payments could be subject to income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I ask, from where is this additional revenue to come? Let us combine this measure with another promise or position advanced in the House during the current session, namely, that there should be universal old age security payments of $150 a month. The first proposal would pay family allowances at the rate of $15 a month for those under 16, $20 a month for those 16 and 17, on a universal basis. The implementation of these two programs would require an additional expenditure of about $1.5 billion in excess of the presently projected costs I have already mentioned. Do those in the opposition who talk about the burden on the middle income group really believe that the middle income group can be misled to believe that these promises will not cost them money?
I have not finished costing some of the proposals of those in the opposition. Some have talked about the desirability of a guaranteed annual income, a concept which I have indicated before the government is continuing to consider. We already use the guaranteed income technique in the income supplement for the aged and we are now about to apply it to family allowances. In addition, we have created a fund in conjunction with interested provincial governments which will be used to finance experiments on a full guaranteed income technique.
However, to move immediately to a full nation-wide guaranteed income would require enormous new finan-

June 29, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
cial resources. Even if paid only at the poverty line levels set out in the 1969 Economic Council brief to the Senate committee on poverty, which numerous councils and agencies have suggested are already outdated, such a full program would cost anywhere from an additional $1.5 billion to $2 billion taking into account all savings from present programs, including savings from the recent guaranteed income supplement increases for the aged and the projected FISP expenditures. I have picked a conservative figure of $1.5 billion to $2 billion based on outdated poverty line levels.
Let us add it all up. Those who advocate a universal old age security payment of $150 a month are advocating an increased expenditure of $700 million to $800 million. Those who advocate universal family allowance payments at maximum FISP benefit levels are advocating an additional $700 million of federal spending. Those who advocate a guaranteed income, even at 1969 Economic Council levels, are advocating an additional expenditure of $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion. The projected expenditure of $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion for a guaranteed income would be over and above what is now being spent. It would be over and above the increased spending resulting from the two guaranteed income supplement increases for the aged voted in the last two years and would be over and above the money allocated to FISP. This brings us to a rather grand price tag at the level of $3 billion to $3.5 billion in extra federal expenditures.
It would only be fair to go into how those in the opposition who suggest this very extensive increase in our expenditures for income security would fund these proposals. On the basis of the promises already advanced by the opposition, I believe that when we analyse the inadequacy of their responses to this question we will see that they are really insulting the intelligence of middle income Canadians.
This government accepts that the burden of financing new programs should be spread fairly and equitably. I think the Family Income Security Plan will reflect this philosophy. Only 28 per cent of the revenue required to finance FISP will come directly from families with children who must give up all or part of their present family allowances. The remaining 72 per cent will come from general revenue. This means corporations, childless couples and single people as well as families with children. In short, everyone will bear a proportion of this task.
What I pointed out in Quebec and re-emphasize now is that even if we were to increase the tax rate on high income earners and on corporations to extreme proportions, the revenue generated would be greatly inadequate to finance the new large-scale programs advocated by various members of the opposition. I was simply pointing out where we must look for the needed revenue if the promises of many of these politicians are to be realized. Do any in this House seriously think the middle income groups in this country can be so easily manipulated that they will believe that promises and policies such as I have heard in the House would not cast a partial burden upon them?
I might refer to a recent speech by the leader of the New Democratic Party when he talked about where we might find some additional revenue. He talked about obliterat-

ing any tax concessions to corporations as a fetchingly appealing strategy. Unfortunately, it will soon come home that even that by doing that not enough revenue would be generated to anywhere near finance proposals of this magnitude. I have pointed out that, on the basis of rough estimates, steep increases in corporation tax, in the order of say 20 per cent, would yield only $400 million to $500 million. I have also pointed out that just a $10 universal increase in the old age pensions from $80 to $90, a woefully inadequate figure in itself, would eat up approximately half of that amount.
Some of the opposition talk of taxing the rich to implement this promise. I repeat, of course we should: However, 1969 statistics show that only 11 per cent of the Canadian taxpayers paid on incomes of over $10,000 a year.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: We know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
It is a fact. Even if this is but a rough guide, it hardly indicates a sufficient tax base to render adequate revenue to the government, even at prohibitive tax rates. I frankly feel that if we taxed in full every dollar earned over $20,000 we would get but a fraction of the amount necessary for the large-scale programs mentioned.
In light of these facts, I realize that some of those in the opposition will admit that even if we applied prohibitive tax rate increases against the affluent it would not bring in enough revenue for all the increases they are suggesting. But then, of course, at least in respect of FISP they would go on to suggest special recovery rates, especially if we made universal payments to the middle income groups.
In setting these recovery rates the opposition has a choice. They can recover at rates of up to 100 per cent, or, if they are afraid of further alienating the middle-income voter, which they greatly desire not to do, they can recover at much lower levels.
If they do not recover at rates of up to 100 per cent there will be a major leakage of benefits to the affluent in this country and there will also be a heavy additional burden on the general revenue fund, the bulk of which comes, once again, from the middle income group which they claim they want to rescue from the burden of increased taxation. If, for example, they recover at normal tax rates, then that recovery would represent only slightly in excess of $200 million of the additional $700 million needed to pay universal benefits-a loss of close to $500 million which could otherwise be directed to other more pressing social concerns, as well as a substantial burden on the middle income groups, as I have just pointed out. If, on the other hand, they did recover at rates of 100 per cent, then all they would be doing would be placing an additional tax burden on the middle and upper income husband in order to make a payment to his wife.
So once more let us review the opposition proposals in their totality: new additional federal spending programs of up to $3.5 billion, with little prospect of obtaining a significant proportion of this money from increased levies on the rich and the corporations, even at prohibitive rates.
June 29, 1972

Thus it is obvious that those opposition members to whom I have referred are already advocating increased taxation affecting the middle income groups.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: What about the other income groups?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
With regard to the upper income groups and the corporations I have already said that to finance this proposal-and they will pay their share-taxation would have to be levelled at much higher, even at prohibitive rates.
So when opposition members make charges of irresponsibility, let them, to avoid charges of disdain for the intelligence of Canadian taxpayers, tell the middle income group where they intend to raise the money to carry out the promises they are making. Let them be assured of one thing: these middle income Canadians are not so naiVe that they will not ask the question. I believe this is a challenge which the opposition must meet.
For the benefit of those who talk about the burden of some of our policies on the middle income group I should point out just in what way certain of our policies have helped the middle income group.
For example, we have not forgotten to provide financial compensation to middle income citizens with families. Our income tax laws continue to provide for children's exemptions. This is because they are mainly directed to horizontal redistribution of the tax burden from taxpayers who have children to taxpayers who do not. Tax exemptions for children are estimated to represent $550 million. The tax exemption system does favour middle and higher income families because, as income is higher, the exemption becomes more valuable.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Right on!

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Nor is this the only government measure which aids the middle income group. I would cite for example, programs such as hospital insurance, medicare, unemployment insurance, the Canada Pension Plan, retirement, disability, widows' and orphans' benefits, and the financing of post-secondary education, all of which were implemented under Liberal governments.
These have spared those benefiting by them enormous personal financial obligations which might otherwise have crushed their financial security and forced them into a dependency on welfare. This is especially true since programs such as hospital insurance, medicare and postsecondary education financing have been most heavily utilized by the middle income groups in comparison with all other income groups in our society.
In this connection I should stress that our country has outperformed the United States, despite their vastly superior financial resources. We have not only kept pace with the American economy and the American standard of living, notwithstanding the extra pressure of a proportionately faster growing labour force, but we have also provided social benefits not yet available in the United States, for example, comprehensive universal hospital insurance and medicare, basic non-contributory old age pensions and family allowances.
Moreover, we should remember that thanks to the prosperity resulting from the improvement of the economy in
Family Income Security Plan
the last decade, a process toward which present government and Liberal governments preceding it have greatly contributed, real income flowing to the middle income group, over and above the inflation factor, has risen by almost 30 per cent. In short, thanks to positive government economic measures much of our working class has moved into the middle income group. And through continued vigorous government action we intend to see that these workingmen who have moved into the middle income group stay there.
I should also like to talk about a few of the other criticisms which have been levelled at the Family Income Security Plan. First, I would point out that its key principle is to assist the low income worker. Thus it goes a long way toward meeting a number of criticisms of our present welfare system.
This plan is not designed to aid the indolent. Its principal aim, I repeat, is to aid those who work, to build in incentives which will encourage them to continue working by providing supplementation to their low-level earnings.
We hear today much criticism on the grounds that people are sometimes placed in situations which encourage them to ask: Why should I work when I can get as much on welfare? The middle income group feels it has worked hard and saved its money. Naturally it resents those who would abuse the welfare system and prefer to use the hard-earned middle income tax dollar to support themselves without working.
Of course, as I have often stated, the number of people who would prefer to live on welfare rather than work is exaggerated. But the feeling held by many people is understandable, none the less. There are some who would prefer to live on welfare and turn down reasonable job opportunities.
The Family Income Security Plan helps meet this problem by providing incentives for the low income earner. It assists him or her to resist the temptation, if and when it does exist, to go on welfare and withhold his or her contribution to society.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: How does the bill do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: If the criticism about some social assistance rates being as high as or higher than certain wage levels is justified, it is derived from the fact that in some provinces social assistance rates applicable to a family with several children often do come perilously close to what the minimum wage rates or laws provide in that province.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Anything is possible with this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I could easily talk about some provincial governments of the same political complexion as the hon. member which do the same thing. This closeness between welfare and the minimum wage is especially true when one considers that often other social services, such as hospitalization and medicare, are provided to the man or woman with a family on social assistance while the wage earner must pay the regular shot. FISP does something about this.

Family Income Security Plan Mr. Alexander: The minister is filibustering his own bill.
June 29, 1972

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: It builds in incentives for workers to remain in the work force by providing incremental income. The wage structure in Canada does not take into account the dependency factor.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Order, please. I would suggest to hon. members to my left that there is so much noise and interruption that it might be deemed to be somewhat unfair to the minister who is trying to make his speech. I think the minister should be given an opportunity to make his speech without all these interruptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, in terms of incentives the wage structure in Canada does not take into account the dependency factor. An employer pays the same rate to the married man or woman with a family as to the single man or woman for the same job and the same duties. Therein lies the problem.
Social assistance rates leave a large gap between the level paid to a single man or woman and the level of income that the single man or woman can earn by working. So, to a much greater degree, incentives are preserved. It is where the man or woman has a family that social assistance levels sometimes approximate minimum income wage rates. This results from a legitimate desire on the part of the welfare system not to penalize the child or children of the welfare recipient. And this-the position of a family on assistance-is where the disincentives emerge as a real problem.
FISP recognizes the problem. It gives meaningful income supplementation to the low income wage earner. It recognizes that his or her earnings are low and boosts the total family income according to his or her family responsibilities. In other words, it takes into account the number of children, a factor that the wage structure, by its very nature, cannot do.
The importance of this principle of wage supplementation was brought up again in the latest report of the National Council of Welfare which restressed the profile of Canadian poverty. The basic fact is that the majority of Canada's poverty population comes from the working poor group, those in marginal, seasonal, interrupted or part-time employment.
I should now like to refer to one other criticism made by some members of the opposition of the Family Income Security Plan, namely, that somehow the FISP application form and cheque will constitute some form of stigma as well, as some have indicated, as an administrative nightmare.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Let hon. members hear the explanation. Potential FISP beneficiaries will fill out a simple income form, just as impartial and anonymous as and simpler than the income tax forms millions of Canadians now fill out. On the return voyage-the arrival and cashing of the FISP cheque-the stigma is non-existent as well. The amount of the cheque alone is no indicator of income, since a person would have to know the number and ages of the recipient's children before he could begin to calculate the person's income. The cheque will be a government

of Canada cheque, as are millions of cheques received by beneficiaries of other government programs, such as unemployment insurance, old age security, Canada Pension Plan, manpower training allowances, and, of course, the regular pay cheques issued by the federal government to its employees. Finally, the only people who need know the amount of the cheque are those who cash it, and I do not think Canadian banks are in the habit of announcing the details of the financial dealings of their customers.
This will not be our first experience with cheques issued under a selective benefit program. We have had five years' experience with the guaranteed income supplement for the aged, which is now received by more than one million senior citizens, and we have not heard loud cries of outrage that this cheque stigmatizes the pensioners.
Why should there be? The income test under the guaranteed income supplement is impersonal; it is a matter strictly between the administering authorities and the person concerned. The test is conducted by mail, and payments are made by cheque which can be promptly cashed or deposited in any one of the many and conveniently distributed branches of Canada's banking system. Why, then, should there be a social stigma under the Family Income Security Plan?
With regard to the question of administrative complexity, may I make just a few comments. I frankly admit that the administration of the plan is, of course, more complex than the rather simplistic approach to universal payments. However, the main principles of FISP are not at all difficult to comprehend. The amount of benefits payable is not difficult to comprehend; the ages determining the amount of benefits are not difficult to comprehend; the concept of basic income levels or thresholds is not difficult to comprehend. Neither is the idea that an income test similar in principle to income taxation is used to determine eligibility, or the application of this simple income test on one application form, as is the case with the guaranteed income supplement. I believe all these points are easy to understand.
In conclusion, may I point out that the Family Income Security Plan is but one facet of an over-all government program to deal constructively with employment generating policies and with poverty. These priorities fall into three categories among the Canadian population. First, there are those Canadians who are permanently out of the work force. They are one priority. When we review government policies designed to assist this group I think it can be established that this group is treated better under this government than the same group would be in any country of the free world comparable to Canada. Let me just analyse the people in this group. There are the aged, and for these we have provided the guaranteed income supplement. For the disabled we cost-share support payments under the Canada Assistance Plan.
The second category is the working poor, for whom we have designed policies, of which FISP is a major ingredient, to assist them; I have already listed these policies, in addition, we have the new unemployment insurance plan. We have also raised the minimum wage levels in the federal sphere as well as introduced needed labour legislation to protect these workers from the ravages of technological change.
June 29, 1972

Lastly, the third category and priority among Canadian citizens is the unemployed. We have directly intervened, in cases where the private sector has not been able to be of assistance, with programs such as Local Initiative, Opportunities for Youth, cost-sharing with the provinces and work activity projects.
I recommend the Family Income Security Plan to the House as an essential ingredient in the necessary over-all attack in terms of giving added income supplementation to the working poor of this country and as a constructive measure to deal with poverty.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). Somebody said he was trying to defend the indefensible, but he reminds me of a goldfish going around and around in a fish bowl and getting nowhere.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: You need a new pair of glasses.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: As a matter of fact, he reminded me a little bit of what Shakespeare said in that he protested far too much. It is interesting to note that he spoke about the things the Liberal government has done over the years but forgot to refer to what that great Prime Minister did who occupied the seats of the mighty for longer than any other man in the British Commonwealth, Prime Minister Mackenzie King. I am sure he did not do that intentionally; in fact, I would never accuse him of really doing anything intentionally. Mackenzie King brought in children's allowances in 1946.

speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) corrects me and I accept his correction, but I think the bill became law in 1946.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: It was passed in 1944 and became law in 1945.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I accept that correction and I note that the hon. member has been reading up on this subject. He was in the House at the time so he has that advantage over the minister and myself.
Why the minister did not refer to this fact when he was boasting so much about what the Liberal party had done over the years is a little hard for me to comprehend. I always try to comprehend what the minister has to say because I get such peculiar answers to the questions I ask him.
The minister referred to OHSIP, the training of doctors, and the health resource fund. I hope I am not going to embarrass him by mentioning these things, but he knows the mess they are in at this time. He is having difficulty all across the country with health resources and the shortage of general practitioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Dr. Potter says there is no shortage.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
The minister does not have to refer to Dr. Potter because he is referring to Ontario. The minister is
Family Income Security Plan
in trouble in every province because of a shortage of doctors, general practitioners; he knows that and that emergency wards are overtaxed. Over and over again I have asked him about this. Once in a while there is a flash of light and the minister seems to see a vision, but then he loses it.
On June 9 the minister said that the next thing he was going to bring in or think about, which should have been brought in before on the recommendation of the Hall Commission, is pharmacare or drug care. Yesterday he forgot about these things and said that we are doing this under the Canada Assistance Plan. He has told me that for the last two or three years. What I want to know is, did he lose his vision of June 9, 1972, again?
Let us go back to all those great things he said the Liberal party was doing. This bill is very complex, ill-conceived and poorly prepared. It is almost impossible to administer and if there is any answer to that I should like to hear it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: You just haven't read it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: No one can. Would it not have been easier to have family allowances payable to everybody and cut back a little on other government spending?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Like what?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I will give you some examples a little later if you will have patience. Let me refer to what Mr. King did and compare it with the situation today. This bill does not provide the economic help the Liberal party gave back in 1944 when it brought in family allowances. If the minister thinks it does I should like him to get up and say so. This bill includes a means test and classifies poverty. It creates different stratas in our society. What financial help does it give the mothers of this country? I suggest it gives less than the measure adopted in 1944. The minister did not tell the mothers they were going to get less. Let us be clear about that. But he underestimates them.
In 1946 the average industrial wage was just over $30 per week and in 1970 it was just over $130 per week, four times as much or a 400 per cent increase. It does not take a mathematician to compare the purchasing value of the two figures. FISP will pay $180 in respect of children up to age 12, and it will pay $240 in respect of those from 12 to 18 years of age. All FISP does is restore a portion of the purchasing value of the dollar; yet the minister makes a great deal out of what he is doing for the unfortunate poor. Even those entitled to the maximum now will have less in purchasing power than people had originally under the previous family allowance scheme. That scheme was universal; this is not. People will be much worse off, so this is nothing more than a pious platitude or a crying epitaph to a vanishing allowance.
Approximately one-third of those now receiving family allowances will be cut off entirely. About one-third will be receiving the maximum. I should like to know why the $4,500 income bracket was chosen as the most deserving. As far as I know the minister gave no reason for choosing this figure. Why is the $9,100 income bracket the least deserving? About one-third will get the full allowance. About half of the remainder will get less than they do

Family Income Security Plan under the present scheme and the other half will get a little more.
I think we must keep in mind that this bill was first advanced in 1970 but is not going to come into force until 1973. I should like hon. members to remember that the minister first advanced this scheme in 1970 but nothing will take place until June, 1973. What will be the result of inflation in the meantime? If inflation continues at the 10 per cent rate over two and a half years the $20 the minister is talking about will only be worth $18. I notice the minister is making note of this so I hope he will have a change of heart and increase the amount.
Just a short time ago the minister announced that this legislation would be in effect this fall. A week or so later he said it would not be operative until next year. In the space of one week he doubled the time for it to become operative. This is why I wonder whether or not the government knows what it is doing. What information did the minister have when he made the statement that it would be in effect this fall? What information did he have at that time which he did not have previously? I think that is a very pertinent question. Why did he then change the date from the fall until next June? What was his reasoning? In September of 1971 he said it would be operative in May of this year. Does anyone really know when it will be operative? Why was it necessary to hire outside help? Why did th eminister find it necessary to hire experts and consultants from outside in order to tell him how to run the computer.
The minister boasted about what the government has been doing in respect of unemployment insurance and so on. The minister has been in the House only about half the time, but long enough surely to have heard over and over again the questions about people who were having difficulty getting their unemployment insurance payments and were almost starving. If this is an example of the Liberal philosophy of being good to the poor, it is a different philosophy from that of the Conservative party.
As I said before, the experts and consultants had to tell the department how to run the computer. One of the higher-ups in the minister's department said, "Well, it is the computers; we got into a mess in respect of unemployment insurance because of the computers; it was a catastrophe". This makes one wonder whether this bill will be just as great a catastrophe.
Let us take another look at the defects of this poorly drawn and poorly drafted bill. If a worker started with an income of $4,500 in 1970, with the ordinary increase in salary he would receive he would not qualify for the full benefits by the year 1973. He would be paying more money in income tax and would be taxed on the FISP benefits he would receive simply because he would be receiving less money from FISP. In reality this is a tax. This will continue all the way up the scale until he is pushed to the cut-off level at which he will not be eligible. As poverty increases more and more, as it has in the last few years, people will be beyond the cut-off level and less payments will be made in respect of children's allowances.
The minister was not in the House at the time, but I am sure some of his colleagues who are sitting here were, when Mr. Pearson as Prime Minister came into the House in 1963 and announced the very bright philosophy about which the minister spoke this morning to the effect that poverty would be ended. Unfortunately, it has become worse.

speechtext: Tell us about the opposition of the Conservatives in 1944.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
If you are asking for it I will give it to you before I am through. I will tell you about the mess you made of medicare and a few other things in this country as well as about unemployment and inflation. You will hear about this if you ask for it. On the other hand, if you want to stick to the subject we are on we will stick to it. As I was saying, more and more people are living below the poverty line. This is the way the minister thinks he will end poverty. He may have bright ambitions, but as a result of my experience in life I can tell him that he is no Lochinvar on a white charger.
The last point I wish to make has to do with the complete absence of any provision for the retarded child. The minister may ask what this has to do with this legislation. He continues going around and around the fishbowl. There is no provision for the provincial guardian or some other responsible party to guard and guide the interests of the child. I have seen many children who have been abused. It is not very long ago that many articles appeared about the battered child syndrome. So far as I can see the minister has done nothing about this. No provision whatever is made for the retarded child who requires extra care. If the minister, with his great humanitarian ideas, wants to do the things he is talking about let him bring in a provision to pay for the care of retarded children who are in the home. These children require extra care. Once they go to an institution the government is faced with an expense of$10to$15a day. Why does the minister not bring in some provision in this regard and add it to this bill if he really has a humanitarian attitude toward these people? There is no provision whatsoever for the child who is retarded and requires extra care in cases where the parents look after him in their own homes at their own expense instead of shoving him off to an institution at the expense of the public. These people do not receive a cent.
I say to the minister that his bill falls far short of what was done in 1945. At that time payments were made universal. Now he is picking out about a third of the people to help and is doing less for them because of the purchasing value of the dollar. I think the minister should redraft his speech before the public become aware of it.
I wish to refer now to the filling out of the tax reform sheet and what amounts to a tax of 33 cents on every $100 of additional income. In my opinion this is a complete nightmare. The minister obviously does not understand

June 29, 1972

the bill. I say that with all kindness in my heart because as I looked over the figures I could not understand them either. I asked some other people to look at them and they did not understand them. The minister has already proven that even his experts do not understand this provision or are afraid of the computer because they do not know how it is to be fed the information.
The minister postponed this measure until this June and then until perhaps next June. He goes around and around the merry-go-round. He talks about the poor and about taxing the middle class more. If the minister did not say this I will accept his word for it. However, the Montreal Gazette and some other papers thought he was really after the middle class and would reduce them to serfdom. Whether or not the minister really meant that or whether or not he really said it, it is a fact that the middle class people are the ones who will be properly soaked by taxation.
The government refers with piety to its humanitarian instinct and says that all things that are good come from their party. As I look across at them and remember how well they hid the fact that they will increase taxes next year by 3 per cent, I deny their humanitarianism. The minister did not include that in his speech this morning when he was defending the middle class. Whatever the minister's feelings may be, he is part of a government that is increasing taxation for the middle class next year by 3 per cent.
I should like to comment now on these new income tax forms. Every time a person's salary goes up or down he must report it. Every time a person's salary or a person's commission goes down and he finds himself in difficulties because of decreased income and applies for help which he needs immediately, how long will it take to reach him? I ask the minister, if a fellow applies in 1970 will he not get help until 1973? If a fellow finds that his income is cut and he needs the money now, how long will it take before he gets it? I think that is a very fair question.
I do not want to go into further details and embarrass the minister because he is in a sufficiently bad position now. However, let me point out that people must fill in these forms every time their income goes up or down. It is like a yoyo. Once the form arrives in Ottawa nobody will be able to figure it out so they will put it into the computer and then the fellow will be told either that he will get less money next year or a little more. Where are these records to be checked? Believe it or not, they are to be checked in the income tax branch. I remember, as many in the House do, when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) accused the government of attempting to do that very thing, but it was denied. Hon. members can check this in Hansard. However, we were told in committee that this is the very thing they are going to do in relation to this measure. These are Gestapo tactics, with a Gestapo checking financial returns that are supposed to be completely secret.
I spoke about the person who really needs help. In the majority of cases it is my opinion that FISP will pay too much or too little each year. There will be one heck of a mess. In the majority of cases incomes will be going up
Family Income Security Plan
and down like a yoyo. As I said, the process will be computerized and it will be only as good as the people who are feeding data into the computer. Since the information will be changing continually, the computers will get mixed up. This will be no better than Information Canada, and it has been a great disappointment to the people running it. I could go on about a few other things that have been great disappointments.
This measure was brought in with loud cheers from the government supposedly to help the poor more than the rich, but it does not do this. A family with an income of $3,000, paying no income tax and with one child, will get $180 from FISP, but a family with an income of $60,000 and one child will get an extra $184. How in the world can the minister tell me that the plan does more for the poor than for the rich? It seems to me that the only sane thing to do is to make the family allowance universal and to cut back on welfare payments for children by an equal and offsetting amount. The government has just taken us into another jungle of computers from which it will be difficult to extricate ourselves, and already they are in a mess, so far as computers are concerned, with the social security measures they have brought in.
I could refer to medicare and talk at length of the mess there which they do not know how to get out of. They do not know whether to get more doctors because costs are going up and up and they cannot meet them. As I have said before, they do not know what to do with emergency departments in hospitals. So they are in an all-round jungle.
It is my belief that all this should be brought under one department. For instance, why should $30 million be spent on the administration of a program that is supposed to help the poor? This is exactly what is being done, with a doubling of the staff. The minister failed to point this out in his speech. I hope he will correct this when he goes on the hustings. I hope he will tell the people just how bad this bill is.

Perhaps the solution could be found by scrapping income tax exemptions for dependent children, scrapping government handouts for public housing and increasing family allowances to cover all these things and make sure that we deal fairly with everybody and that we keep in mind that family allowances are for children. supposed to be protected. I am sorry to see the government in this age of affluence bringing in a bill that does much less for the poor people of this country than was done in 1945.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) I felt rather sad. It is always sad to watch a man's tortuous anguish as his once kind heart is at war with his guilty conscience, for that was the background of his speech this morning, and it is the background of the speeches he has made recently across the country.
This poor, sad minister, who would like to go down in history as a great friend of the ordinary Canadian, is being ground to dust by the reactionaries who accompany him in the cabinet of Canada. And as is always the case, Mr. Speaker, if you allow yourself to be ground down by ideas and thoughts in which you do not believe, you end up by accepting those ideas and thoughts and becoming just as reactionary as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and other ministers in the Cabinet.
The minister's speech this morning was a remarkable exercise in lack of logic, in lack of sense and indeed, Mr. Speaker, in lack of honesty. When he was trying to show how much everybody wanted he included not only the additional cost under FISP for universality that some of us advocate, not only the increases in pension costs, but also talked about a guaranteed annual income, something which has never come into this debate. I just wonder whether he should fire his speech writers and advisers because they stopped short. Why did they not include the cost of housing, the cost of post-secondary education, the cost of pollution, the cost of everything else? He would have had a great budget in that case and he could have beaten his poor breast a little harder. Uriah Heap had nothing on this minister.
Because he is trying to suggest to the middle income groups that he is really their champion, what does he do? I say this with great sadness, and I use strong language. He does the most disgusting thing he could have done, and that is to appeal to the anti-welfare backlash in this country.
If there is any logic at all in what he said, let me say to him that his bill, with the maze and mess administratively that it is, is only an invitation to abuse. Anyone who knows anything at all about law or about administration knows perfectly well that if the administration is simple, abuse is difficult-you cannot get away with anything. But if the administration is complicated, abuse is a lot easier. There are loopholes you can get through. You can deny that you have made $200, that your wife has made $200, or deny other things much more easily than you could have under the previous plan.
The minister knows that a complicated bill will make abuse easier. Then why in heaven's name should he talk about it? Why does he talk about it except to try to throw sand in the eyes of many people who think that this bill is a retrograde step? There are many people in his constituency, many workers in his city, who know that what he is doing in this bill is diddling the people of Hamilton and the people of Canada.

Then he reminds us that only 11 per cent of the people in Canada make incomes over $10,000. We have been saying that to this government and to the Conservative government that preceded it ever since I have been active in politics. We have been saying to these people that the kind of system they promote concentrates income and wealth in an ever smaller group of the population. He is not telling me anything new when he tells me that only 11 per cent-and I am a little surprised it is as high as that- have incomes above $10,000. But what he did not tell us, and what he carefully avoided telling us, is the proportion of the total income in Canada, the percentage of the total wealth in Canada, over which this small group of people actually have control. It is about 30 per cent, compared with his figure of 11 per cent of the population.
FISP is a tax on the middle income groups, and the minister is hypocritical when he warns those groups about taxing them. He is taxing them in this bill when he takes from them the payment that would otherwise have been made to them. It is a regressive tax because it is a tax that falls only on those who have children. That is why it is a regressive and undesirable tax.
Here we are talking about the middle income groups. Ages ago we used to speak about such people being fairly rich, but now we are talking about people making between $7,000 and $11,000 a year, and that in modern society is not very much.
May I remind this minister who undoubtedly reads history, particularly the history of the Liberal party,' with a great deal of attention and pleasure, that when the late Mackenzie King introduced family allowances in the first place he reduced the tax exemption for a child in receipt of family allowance from $500 to $300.
We are told in books that Mackenzie King sometimes consulted certain mediums. May I suggest that this minister consult the ghost of Mackenzie King because even from that gentleman he could learn a great deal, and he has been dead for some years. That is the way to handle this matter. When you have a universal family allowance plan you should deal with the tax system as was done in 1944-45. You do not deal with it as the minister does.
The minister says that all the increases in welfare and in family security that we advocate will cost a lot of money, and asks where will the money come from except from the middle income groups? I want to tell him where it can come from, Mr. Speaker. He is right when he says it could only come from the middle income groups so long as his government is in power, because that is the only place that his government will go for the money.

speechtext: I did not say that.

speechtext:
So long as the squire from Mount Royal is Prime Minister of Canada, the only people who will be taxed will be the middle income groups. But if you had a government that was oriented toward the people of Canada, that was honestly concerned about improving the lot of the ordinary Canadian, there would, let me tell the minister, be no mystery about where the money could come from.
On a national accounts basis this year we are to collect, after the last budget, 50 per cent of our federal revenue
June 29, 1972

from individual taxpayers and only 12 per cent from corporations. Just ten years ago we collected about 41 per cent from individuals and somewhere around 20 per cent from corporations. Twenty years ago we collected about
28	per cent from individual taxpayers and 27 per cent from corporations, and about 25 or 30 years ago we collected about 27 per cent from individuals and 28 per cent,
29	per cent or 30 per cent from corporations. This government and the Tory government that preceded it in 1963 introduced tax systems which have consistently squeezed a larger and larger proportion of federal revenue out of individual taxpayers and consistently reduced the proportion that comes from corporations.
What is the result of this kind of tax system? The result is that in 1969, the latest year for which there are figures, 46 per cent of all Canadian corporations did not pay a single, solitary cent in income tax.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: And people call this a just society.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Of the mining and oil corporations in Canada, 78 per cent did not pay a single sou in income tax to the federal treasury. Poor Shell Oil Company, Mr. Speaker, one of the underprivileged, impoverished multinational corporations of the world, made about $250 million in profits in the five-year period between 1964 and 1969 but did not pay a single, solitary cent in income tax to the federal treasury. One might assume that Shell Oil would be philanthropic; well, it was not. Falconbridge mines in the same period made a profit of about $250 million and paid $15 million in income tax; that represents a tax rate of 6 per cent. And, if that was not enough, the company shortly thereafter obtained a $4 million grant from the federal treasury. That was a gift from the people of Canada to another impoverished corporation in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: How do you like that, Murray? Are you not proud?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
The tax cuts and other goodies the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) provided for the corporations of this country a little while ago will save them $500 million in the first year and $700 million in the second year. He has given them $1.2 billion which they do not need, as profits in the last six months have been going up, up and up without ceasing. They have increased by between 30 per cent and 40 per cent over what they were in the similar period one year ago. The minister has handed $1.2 billion to the corporations. This is money which they do not need, money which will not create any employment, money which has been given to manufacturing and processing concerns that are now working at less than capacity. I say to the government that if that $1.2 billion were used to help the poor in Canada and middle income groups of Canada, not only would there be greater justice in our society but the economy would be a great deal better off and unemployment would be reduced.
I remind the minister also of the handouts this government has given corporations every year. The total amount, including tax concessions, etc., is about $2 billion every year. We have given handouts through the Depart-
Family Income Security Plan
ment of Regional Economic Expansion. According to a preliminary study undertaken by a young professor who did a conscientious job, handouts of $200 million, $300 million and $400 million a year under DREE have brought almost no benefit to the areas of this country concerned. We hand out hundreds of millions of dollars under all sorts of programs. These handouts to corporations altogether total about $2 billion a year, Mr. Speaker. I emphasize this. I say that that is where the money is to be found, that is from where it should come. Let us stop this welfare system for the wealthy corporations of this country, most of them foreign-owned, and let us bring in some welfare for the ordinary people of Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when you look carefully at the budget which the Minister of Finance presented you will arrive at a significant and important conclusion, and if any member of the Liberal party is not shaken by that conclusion he has lost his marbles, lost his humanity, or perhaps lost both.

speechtext:
If he had any
marbles or humanity to begin with.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
When you read the budget speech of the Minister of Finance and peruse the accompanying material, you will find that the corporations of Canada will contribute in 1972-73, on a budgetary basis, 15 per cent of the total federal revenue. If you look at another chart in the budgetary material, you will find that the federal government will pay out 15 per cent of all federal expenditures to the corporations. It will pay that much to them under what is called economic development and support. Economic development and support obviously means various handouts to corporations under DREE, under other development grants, under defence industry programs and includes, I must add, manpower training grants which undoubtedly would be desirable if the program were planned properly.
I want to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to this: Corporations will contribute 15 per cent toward revenues; corporations will take 15 per cent of the expenditures. In the result, the corporations of Canada will contribute nothing at all to family allowances, old age pensions, medicare, hospital insurance programs or to any of those humane schemes that reluctant governments have been forced to put on the statute books. That is the result of this government's policies. One can readily see where the money can be found.
The money is there, Mr. Speaker, the funds are there, the revenues are there, and the necessary wealth is there. This is a great country, a rich country, a wonderful country. The minister cannot do what I assume in his heart he would like to do, namely, deal justly and decently with the people of Canada, because the funds, the wealth, are in the wrong hands. They are in a few corporate hands in this country and the government does not have the guts to open those hands and take for Canada the money that is in them.
Let me tell the minister of another way to obtain revenue. The government could obtain more if it were to reduce unemployment significantly. The Economic Coun-

Family Income Security Plan cil of Canada said two or three years ago that every percentage point of unemployment means a loss to us of $1.5 billion per year. Today that loss is probably slightly more in view of increased prices of various sorts. Every percentage point of unemployment means at least a loss of $1.5 billion. Every $1.5 billion that is lost to us represents a loss to the federal treasury of approximately $500 million, $600 million or $700 million; I do not know exactly how much is lost that way. If unemployment, instead of being at more than 6 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis, were to be down to 3 per cent, the minister would have all the revenue he needs for a proper family allowances plan and a proper old age pension plan, and there would be no need to impose additional taxes on the middle income groups of this country.
What has this government permitted? It has deliberately created loopholes for corporations that cost the treasury about $400 million each year. It has deliberately cut the taxes of corporations, and these tax cuts will cost the treasury $500 million and $700 million a year for two years. We are talking about $1 billion, roughly. It has deliberately given the mining and oil corporations tax holidays without end. These, according to the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), cost the federal treasury between $300 million and $400 million per year. I heard the other day that Steep Rock mines in northern Ontario was very interested in the three-year tax holiday which is given to the mining corporations of Canada. What did that company do? It had what you and I and anybody else would call one mine. It divided this into three parts, opened the first third and got a three-year tax holiday. When that holiday ended it opened the second third and obtained an additional three-year tax holiday. When that was ended it opened the final third and got another three-year tax holiday. So, instead of obtaining a three-year tax holiday it got a nine-year tax holiday, Mr. Speaker. I understand that the operation was a strip mining or surface mining operation. The company is now considering sinking some shafts, calling it a fourth mine and asking for another three-year tax holiday.
The tax system for which this government is responsible makes that kind of tax avoidance possible. It gives these benefits to corporations. It deliberately creates massive unemployment that brings further losses in production and in revenue, and then it stands there and cries shamelessly "where is the money to come from." The money is there, Mr. Speaker. It is there in the corporations. It is there in the country and the government will not do anything about it.
The real problem that faces the minister and the country with respect to social security programs is that for many years, instead of doing the humane and decent thing of adjusting those programs year by year in accordance with the cost of living increase and the standard of living increase, we sat back and let the same inadequate amount be paid year after year for tens of years, as we did in this case. Suddenly we arrive in 1972, an election year, and the government feels that it ought to do something. They sit down and make calculations and find that if they are to increase the $6 that is now paid for the cost of living increase this figure must be increased to $15. Therefore

you get a 150 per cent jump in one year. To increase the $8 now paid for the cost of living increase the figure must be increased to $20. Again there is a 150 per cent increase in one year. That is what is wrong with our system and the way we do things.
If we had increased the $6 to $7 or $7.50 and then to $9 the second year as the cost of living, the gross national product and the standard of living went up, and increased the family allowance year by year in accordance with the increase of wealth in this country, no one would have to make the kind of calculations which the minister had to make this morning. The increase would be related to what is happening in our economy and to prices. The people would have been dealt with fairly.
What good is it to a family whose children are now grown up who were in hardship all the years the $6 meant less and less year after year until we reached 1972 when it does not mean anything at all? What good is it for the family who lived through those hardships without getting the increases? Justice demands universality. Decency demands universality. Unity demands universality.
The miserable excuses which the minister has trotted out in this and other speeches are meaningless. They are without validity and without meaning. They are the hapless cry of a guilty conscience that is now trying to make political hay out of a situation that the minister knows will not come to him. In fact, we are rearing the point which makes it impolite for me to describe precisely the present state.
The minister talked about our fooling the middle income people. We are not trying to fool them. It is a simple fact that many of the voters in the minister's constituency, Hamilton East, who work for Stelco, Defasco, Westinghouse, in other plants or anywhere else will not receive a penny in family allowance. It is shameful and criminal that that is the way we are going to treat a large proportion of the voters in the minister's own riding. That is why he makes the speeches he does. The minister knows perfectly well that those people resent what he is doing to them. They see that he is adding a tax on to them through this bill. Therefore, he is trying to build up a case for himself. No one, even people who are sometimes called tough, will really begrudge a poor, suffering conscience like that of the minister from looking for an excuse and seeking to get out of this terrible, immoral morass into which the minister and his colleagues have gotten themselves. I am really sorry for the minister. He looks like such a nice guy. He talks as though he really wants to do something. However, after his speech is over the substance which he produced is as disappointing as the poor excuses he tried to make.
My colleagues and I see no excuse for the destruction of the principle of universality. We do not see anything which the minister can boast about in bringing up the family allowance to the level at which the cost of living would have brought it up anyway. We see only sadness in a situation which will divide people and again hurt people who ought not to be hurt. The Minister of National Health and Welfare cannot possibly persuade anyone with intelligence and any kind of social conscience that his FISP bill is anything other than a miserable destruction of the important principle of universality, anything other than
June 29, 1972

neglect for a large number of the children of this country, or that it will assist the poor in Canada as they ought to be assisted. All the minister is doing is enabling them to buy as much in 1972 as they were able to buy some 12, 15 or 20 years ago.
I oppose the bill now as I did then. I am only sorry that the minister is engaging in the kind of argument he has advanced. I suggest to him it is saddening and rather undignified to see him in constant convolution trying to make sense and decency out of a bill that has neither.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to speak to the topic now before the House which, to my mind, is one of the most important ever discussed here.
Family allowances were given the Canadian people in 1945, I believe and they have remained practically the same since. In fact, they were increased by approximately $1 whereas the cost of living has gone up by about 300 per cent.
Now, we see that the minister wants to reduce families to the level of dollars because he reduces family allowances to a matter of dollars and cents. The minister does not know where he will get the money needed to pay those allowances.
But families are worth more than dollars. If there is anything truly concrete, truly great, truly noble, the family is. In fact, were it not for the family, governments would not exist. The population is made up of families. The family has the right to live, it needs all the state can do for it. The needs that should be given priority in our economy are those of the family.
All the speeches we have heard the minister deliver on family allowances are imbued with the fear of lack of money to ensure a decent life to the children of Canada from the uncalculable resources the whole country would have to distribute. We rightfully claim that such an approach to the problem of family income security and family allowances is depressing and absurd, even though it represents the thinking of our most intelligent members of Parliament who endeavoured to summarize government policy in a notorious white paper which was communicated to the population a year ago, published after wide research in the fields of university, administration and legislation. Now let us look at the results. They are offering an extra $170 million, a staggering amount for Canada's 7 million children under 17, the third of a population with a national product of $92 billion in 1971-72 and a production of over $100 billion in 1972-73.
They don't know where to get the money! With an increase by $8 billion in the gross national product in 1972-73, they are wondering where they will find money to help families. But they fail to realize that if we give more money to the families through family allowances they will not keep it but they will spend it.
By doing so, we would give a new impetus to the economy. Families would pay 12 per cent sales tax to the feder-
Family Income Security Plan
al government and 8 per cent to the provincial government-I am thinking of the Quebec government-in addition to all kinds of direct and indirect taxes.
We do not know how to raise money, but we forget that payments made to families would be recovered by the treasury.
Mr. Speaker, having increased by $170 million the allowances paid to the 7 million children under 18 and following an increased production of $8 billion for next year, we forget that 50 per cent of Canadians are unemployed and cannot purchase the goods available in stores and warehouses. We must keep in mind that giving money to families will be the best investment ever made in the history of our economy.
We have funds for the Opportunities for Youth program. This morning I received two telegrams from citizens who asked me to see that things are straightened out because some persons have received grants under this program and they are spending it on orgies. We are witnessing the corruption of our youth. There is plenty of money to corrupt youth, but none whatsoever to support families.
But, national production from 1944 to 1945 amounted to $12 billion only and it has increased to $92 billion in 1971. It will reach $100 billion in 1972.
In 1944, an hon. member's basic salary was $4,000 and we are now drawing some $26,000-nearly seven times more. But family allowances have remained at the same rate. In fact, we take decisions according to our judgment and knowledge.
The salaries of members of Parliament and of many other people have kept pace with the ever increasing cost of living, but family allowances have been left aside. What could be more important, more easily perceived and more human than the family, for it constitutes the basis of society.
The revenues of judges, ministers of the Crown, university graduates, accountants, economists are all geared to rise with the cost of living and the national product; but in the case of our children-they account for one third of our population-the same family allowance rates apply as in 1944-45 when the GNP had an estimated value of only $12 billion, seven or eight times less than today. Yet, we live in the year 1972-73.

Therefore, it seems to me that, about a matter of such importance as guaranteed personal and family income, all the members chosen by the people of Canada to represent them in this House, all equally interested in the well-being of every one of the 23 million citizens living in Canada, in their constituencies, should get together because the most important of all economic questions is that one, a guaranteed personal income based on our national product, brought about by the development of our natural and national resources, by means of the capital and the labour invested by the active adults of our land.
If at long last we would realize that the life of our fellow Canadians is as important as the capital and the labour of the makers of our national product, we would at least

have taken the first step towards a balanced economy, a balanced economic security.
In the various sectors of our economy, we could at last hopefully foresee the end of inflation, unemployment and poverty by putting the needed economic blood in the hands of the true consumers who are the families.
But all that, Mr. Speaker, requires the acknowledgment of the first objective of ail government and parliamentary activities: to guarantee the income security and the life of every living citizen, every human being. This is the first objective of our government. The life of the citizens must have priority over capital-the minister should know that-even over labour because where can we find capital and labour if the citizen has no life?
If we protected so much the capital, the guaranteed income and the work of each individual, why should we not take more care of the life of every citizen even if they have neither work nor money? This is the main concern of any sound, honest and logical administration, of any efficient legislation. This is the main question which should interest all government members elected by the same nation numbering about 23 million at the present time, all having the right to live before being entitled to work and to have money.
Life must come before everything. It is because there are citizens that we have a country, provinces and municipalities.
If capital has an existence which differs from that of human beings, if work exists as an expression of man, life is the foundation of this man's existence and the base of his work or of his capital. Without life, capital and work are impossible for a citizen.
Life deserves our attention; it must be the first objective of our national economic administration as it is the first expression of each citizen's existence even before he is able to work or own capital.
Life first, work afterwards. Is this the order we follow in the hierarchy of our administrative priorities? It is not surprising that there is a lack of economic balance, that capital has to cope with inflation, that work is affected by the changes in the unemployment rate and that the lives of citizens are threatened by the obtrusive presence of dishonouring and depressing poverty.
This is a situation which prevails in many Canadian families. This is how the more we progress the more we go backward in the battle against inflation, unemployment and poverty. We simply take everything backward and cannot see straight. We try to protect capital and work before protecting the citizen. We are considering the scale of values the wrong way. We think we are going up but we continue to slide. Mr. Speaker, this is where we must intervene with all our might, with all our being. We must claim respect for our legal family rights and the establishment of the genuine just society for the family. This is why everywhere capital becomes more and more important, in volume and in revenue, to the detriment of personal incomes which are increasingly taxed, to the detriment of the way of life of citizens without work or money, who become more and more impoverished by the rising cost of

living. Citizens too young, too old, too sick are unable to earn their living either through work or through capital.
We are rich, Mr. Speaker, and we live in poverty. The hon. minister should understand that. This can be remedied by the simple conversion of the guaranteed personal income, by the vital personal right of each family, taking into account the decision we will reach here, in Parliament, the members elected by the people of Canada for a period of five years ending around mid-July 1973.
The decision is up to us; no other citizen of Canada can be held responsible for this decision. Everybody has had the chance to have his say in the many royal commissions held in the last ten years. Research councils and white papers have done their job. Now is the hour of action, of legislation, of administration, in short, the establishment of a new economic order which depends on us only.
If capital is very well treated by every kind of companies and labour unions, the fact remains that every citizen's right to live must be defended with energy and protected permanently by the provisions of Bill C-170 which cannot be adopted without due consideration.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, the House is already aware of the government's interest in all matters affecting cultural development in Canada. In the past few years this interest has become apparent in areas such as publishing, museums, films, the purchase of collections and the award of grants to cultural institutions. Other matters are being studied, some of which are of such importance that certain acts will have to be amended and we shall table these amendments in the House at the appropriate time.
Some time ago we were informed of a suggestion which will certainly interest the House of Commons. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) decided some time ago to offer to the University of Saskatchewan his collections of documents, books and other items relating to his term of office. The university expressed the desire, not only to accept these collections, but to locate them in a setting worthy of their importance. In order to do so it would be necessary to construct a building on the university campus at a cost of some $600,000. The organizers of this project are making every effort to obtain half of this sum from the private sector and they propose that the remaining $300,000 be contributed by the federal government. This suggestion has been studied by our services and negotiations are now under way between the Public Archives, the University of Saskatchewan and the Department of the Secretary of State.
On the basis of this suggestion, I have asked the officials of the Department of the Secretary of State to submit to me a general policy on the question of documents which prime ministers decide to donate to private institutions, as was done by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett whose papers are now deposited in the archives of the University of New Brunswick.
However, while these negotiations are still taking place, I wish to inform the House of Commons that the government is most willing to continue its discussions with the University of Saskatchewan, so that the right hon. member's very generous gift can be placed in a setting appropriate to the important contribution he has made to the development of this country.
