subsubtopic: EMPLOYEES-PROPOSED CHANGES IN PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the President of Canadian National Railways that the company is announcing today that pensions, including pensions received by widows, will be increased to take into account increases in the cost of living since 1969.

Members may recall that effective January 1, 1971, Canadian National pensions were increased by 2 per cent for each year of retirement up to 1969, and in some cases by a larger percentage. The increases to be announced by the company today will, from January, 1972, add 4 per cent to all current pensions that were in force on December 31, 1970; and 2 per cent to current pensions that first came into force during the year ending December 31, 1971. Combined with the action taken in 1971, the effect is that CN pensions will have been increased by 2 per cent for each year of retirement throughout the period 1935-71. I am also informed that the General Chairmen's Association, representing all union members in CN, has submitted proposals for changes in the company's pension plan and these proposals are currently under discussion by the CN Pension Board. Among them is one to escalate pensions because of the higher cost of living.
The announcement by Canadian National of increased pensions is in response to that proposal and to the strong representations made by the General Chairmen on the Pension Board that action be taken as quickly as possible. I might add, parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, that undoubtedly there were strong pressures from this House, as well. The Pension Board has expressed the view that similar adjustments of existing pensions should be made in the future. I understand the union members of the Pension Board welcome this response to their representations.
With regard to the pension formula and other improvements proposed by the General Chairmen's Association, their representatives on the Pension Board are hopeful that further changes to the pension rules will follow. Mr. MacMillan advises me that historically changes proposed by the Pension Board have been implemented. In any event, negotiations with unions representing major groups of employees are due to open well before the year end, at which time any unresolved question is expected to be a bargaining issue.
Having regard to on-going discussions in the Pension Board and the opening of negotiations in the fall, I hope that all hon. members will agree that these matters should be left to labour and management to be resolved in that process. The President of CN also informs me that several changes have been made in the Pension Plan and its administration, through agreement reached through the Pension Board, since the 1970 report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. One of those changes I have already mentioned: the 1971 escalation of 32,000 pensions. In addition, early retirement rules were improved; the 1959 plan was again reopened to members of the 1935 plan and 9,000 employees transferred; age and service requirements for survivor benefits were eliminated for employees killed in the performance of duty and the Pension Board has been reconstituted to give equal representation to union and management, with each side including a pensioner in its membership and designating a co-chairman. In 1972, the company's costs for pension plans are expected to be at least $50 million, an increase of $17 million, or 50 per cent over the last two years.
June 29, 1972

Mr. Speaker, we in this party welcome the minister's announcement of the long overdue increases in Canadian National pensions. I think it is a tribute to the workings of the parliamentary system that there was unanimous support for this from all sides of the House. As a result of the report on pensions the Standing Committee brought down some years ago, and through the efforts of the minister, this breakthrough has been accomplished. I hope that benefits will continue to flow from this report in the years to come.
The increase in pensions will be welcomed by all those pensioners whose pensions, which were far from adequate when they were first established, have been eroded because of inflation which has gone unchecked for the past four or five years. These increases will be welcome news for them, but I point out to the minister that they are little enough. These increases do not offset increases in the cost of living, which run between 3.5 per cent and 4 per cent per year, nor will they offset any purchasing power pensioners have lost over the years as a result of inflation.
I am encouraged by the statement that the matter of escalating pensions is to be a continuing subject of discussion by the Pension Board. I am hopeful the minister will use his influence to persuade the pension board that the very least that should be built into the CNR pension plan is a provision for the automatic escalation of pensions to cover the cost of living. It is an anomalous and distressing situation that these pensioners should be the pawns of Parliament and have to come to us hat in hand to ask for increases in their pensions which should be given to them as a matter of right because of the inflationary situation we have today. I hope the minister will use his influence to persuade the pension board to recommend that this provision be built into the CN pension plan.
I also hope that the minister will use his influence with the Canadian Pacific Railways. The CPR is not mentioned in the minister's statement, naturally, but I hope the minister will be able to prevail upon the CPR to take some action.
I am a bit disturbed by the announcement concerning the pension plan for those now employed by CNR. It is stated that since this matter will come up for negotiation this fall, probably we should leave it this way. Representations were made during the committee hearings. The union took the position that pension adjustments or increases were properly a matter for negotiation. After talking to CNR workers, my impression is that they Eire not satisfied the pension scheme has been given proper attention in negotiations. I strongly urge the minister to consider this matter. If something satisfactory does not develop as a result of the negotiations this fall, some action must be taken to protect the employees who feel they are not being given a proper break. This escalation provision should be built into their pension scheme so that escalation becomes a matter of right.
I congratulate the minister on this announcement. I ask him not to rest here, but to continue to press the CNR and CPR to bring their pension schemes up to a comparable level with those which prevail in industry.

This statement is reasonably lengthy. It makes many references to matters still under discussion about which something might be done in the future. It also recites, as a matter of history, a number of things that have been done in the past couple of years. However, with regard to what was announced today in terms of actual dollars and cents, all we have been told is that the arrangement to escalate CNR pensions by 2 per cent for each year of retirement has been brought up to date by two years. That is all it does. This means that those who got the increase that was provided a little over a year ago will receive increases based on 2 per cent per year or for the two years, 4 per cent but that does not mean 4 per cent of what they are now getting. It is 4 per cent of their basic pension which was established years ago. It means that those who retired in 1970 will get a 4 per cent increase, while those who retired in 1971 will get a 2 per cent increase. That is all it does, and the minister has the gall to say that this is being done to enable these pensioners to cope with the increase in the cost of living. Even old age pensions and veterans pensions are being increased in accordance with the actual rise in the cost of living or in other words, by 3.6 per cent. But these retired employees are being asked to settle for 2 per cent in a year in which the cost of living increased by 3.6 per cent, or 4 per cent over two years in which the cost of living increased by 7 or 8 per cent or more.
I therefore say to the minister that though, like the last speaker, I am prepared to welcome anything which is given to pensioners, when it will amount only to a dollar or two a month, as it will in many cases, I am sure he will not expect me to shout for joy; I am sure he will not think it incumbent upon me to express great appreciation of what has been done. I think the minister should go back to his office, get Mr. Norman MacMillan on the phone and tell him this is not good enough. A lot more has to be done.

Escalation of the pensions of employees must be related to the cost of living. It is not good enough to give a 2 per cent increase when the cost of living goes up by 3 or 4 per cent. subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was stating the family's basic principles and prerequisites. I was saying that the human being is the most important aspect in society, as a divine creature, with aspirations and spiritual and material requirements, and that it has inalienable rights which must be respected and safeguarded.
I was saying as well that the most important duty of a democratic government within society is to give the

people the type of public administration they want, provided it is physically feasible and normally acceptable.
As regards family allowances, we are aware that it is physically possible to provide all Canadian families with family allowances geared to the increase in the cost of living. That is where our views differ from those of the hon. minister; we belong to those who have been asking for a long time for the increase in family allowances, not only for a designated group of families, but for all regardless of race, colour or language. They are human beings who deserve the highest possible consideration from their leaders.
We regret those complex aspects which were brought into Bill C-170. The decreasing rate is unacceptable because it is the money of the community, which must be spent by the community and not only by a group. The children from families whose annual income is below $4,500 are certainly entitled to adequate allowances properly tailored to the cost of living because an annual income of $4,500 is not sufficient.
Even an income between $4,500 and $8,000 is still too low. Families adjust their expenditures to their revenues. The higher their income, the more they spend; and the more they spend, the stronger the economy. In order to solve the problem of poverty, do we have to strip the poor man to help his poorer fellow?
This bill does not leave any room for the fight against poverty. Family allowances were designed to help Canadian families raise their children, the most important resource in our country. This objective becomes fuzzy the moment family allowances are made selective; everyone knows it would be impossible to pay family allowances large enough to compensate for all the expenses needed to raise children. The hon. minister stated in one of his speeches that more than a million Canadian families would not benefit at all from the legislation.
Is there any member here or any Canadian who believes that there are more than a million wealthy families in this country? Does the minister really believe it is fair not to give anything to the children of more than a million Canadian families? Does he really believe there are more than a million families in Canada which do not need any assistance to bring up their children?
Mr. Speaker, this shows the injustice generated by the bill now before us. We would have much to add about this but we say to the minister that he is making a big mistake and creating the greatest social injustice a country has ever known in having this House pass a legislation like the one before us now.
Every family in this country must benefit from this legislation. Whatever their income, all our families need family allowances.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN

But if there are shortages we must leave all necessary economic and monetary powers to the family so they may fulfill their possibilities; the community must distribute

its money among all citizens. Every child of any family in this country is entitled to family allowances.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I say that when we consider Bill C-170 we must consider the entire aspect of redistribution of wealth. Family allowances were established on the principle of universality back in 1946, I believe. Through this bill we shall in a sense redistribute money throughout the various regions of Canada and among the lower income groups of our society. This program, in seeking to implement the theory that it is the government's duty to redistribute the wealth of the people, will turn the universal family allowance concept which was first adopted in 1946 into an additional welfare program. If we accept that, we must then ask, how much will the program cost? It will cost the people of our country an additional $150 million according to the minister. Whom will it benefit? Will it reduce welfare, or perpetuate it? Will it reduce poverty, or contribute to it? I believe this program will perpetuate welfare and poverty since it will encourage people who can least afford large families to raise large families.
Young people growing up in a welfare atmosphere become accustomed to it. They are satisfied to live that way and for a great part of their lives accept welfare and the dole. It is wrong, morally, to do this in a nation as wealthy as Canada, a nation populated with energetic people. As it is, we tax our people too much; we tax our young too much and our old too much. What happens to the middle income groups? They are taxed very heavily, much more heavily, on a proportionate basis, than the wealthy. I think this policy is a mistake.
Before we redistribute wealth on a regional basis we must consider how the various regions of Canada are made up. Which regions will benefit most? How will this money be redistributed? These questions were never answered in committee or during the second reading debate. Perhaps the minister does not know how this is to be done, or is afraid to disclose to the people how our wealth will be redistributed among the regions of this country. This is an important matter, Mr. Speaker, because at the extremities of Canada there is disunity. Before adopting a system that will redistribute wealth we must at this time, for the sake of our survival as a nation, examine how the redistribution is to take place, how it will affect the really rich and the middle classes.
Actually, we have provided a bonus for the married man raising a young family. I am referring, of course, to the previous family allowance plan and to the new FISP plan as well. At present there are income tax exemptions for every child. If we look closely at the system we will see that a married couple with an income of $3,000 per year and one child benefits to the extent of $180 per year from this program. When the income increases to $4,500 the family will receive that $180 and an additional $74 by
Family Income Security Plan
virtue of the reduction in income tax. If the family's income rises to $7,000, its extra spending power diminishes sharply. At $7,000 it obtains little or no benefit from the program. At $9,000 the reduction in income tax is $90. With an income of between $9,000 and $21,000 taxes rise drastically.
However, if you earn between $50,000 and $60,000 you receive almost as great a benefit from the tax system as the man earning $3,000. Clearly, the middle income group shoulders the load. That, I suppose, corresponds with the minister's thinking as expressed in his speech in Quebec. I hold in my hand a copy of the Montreal Gazette of June 21. The following is reported in this newspaper:
Munro said it would be "foolish" to think welfare needs could be met by hitting the "super-rich" and corporations with drastic tax increases.
In other words, he has adopted the Liberal party's concept that we must save the super-rich and tax the middle classes. I wonder if the workers in Hamilton appreciate that. There are many middle income people there. The article continues:
Furthermore, the minister argued that placing too much of a tax burden on the rich could remove the "incentive" to become rich which would leave the government "no further ahead and perhaps worse off."
The report in the Montreal Gazette of June 21 shows that the minister does not think we should tax heavily the super-rich. I used to think Canada was made up mostly of middle income people. The middle class is shrinking. The super-rich, as the minister calls them, and the poor who live at or below the poverty line are increasing. This bill does very little for our shrinking middle class. On the other hand, I think it will perpetuate poverty at the lower end of the income scale. Furthermore, it will permit the super-rich to avoid completely carrying their fair share of the burden in our economy.
Let us consider this redistribution. The committee studying this bill was never informed of any concept or forward-thinking which the department may have worked out as to how the money would be divided between the various regions of Canada. Nor has this House been so informed.
I wish to refer to some figures put forward by Mr. Reuben Baetz, executive director of the Canadian Council on Social Development, with regard to those living below what he and the Economic Council of Canada have established as the poverty level. For a married couple with two children the figure is $3,100, and for a married couple with five children the figure is a little over $5,000. That is what he has classified as the poverty level.
I now wish to refer to the areas which have the greatest number of families living below the poverty line. The figures are as follows: Quebec, 17.5 per cent; Ontario, 12.1 per cent; the prairie provinces, 24 per cent; British Columbia, 14.2 per cent; the Atlantic provinces, 29.7 per cent. There is a great deal of disparity as between the various regions with regard to families living below the poverty line. Has the minister stated that he believes redistribution of wealth as between the various regions under this program will correspond with the program

June 29, 1972
Family Income Security Plan presented by Mr. Baetz in the Economic Council report of 1969? He has not. It should be clearly stated where this redistribution will take place.
Many people attacked Premier Bennett of British Columbia when he stated there should be a redistribution of wealth. I am in complete agreement with that, but it should go directly to the poor people. As I stated, the percentage of poor families in British Columbia is 14.2 per cent, a little better than Ontario and not that much better than Quebec. The prairie provinces and the Atlantic region suffer most in this respect. Will there be a more equitable distribution of wealth under the new family allowance program? I do not believe so.
I wish to refer to some figures in the report concerning unattached individuals living below the poverty line. These figures were established by the Economic Council of Canada and are as follows: the Atlantic provinces, 49.7 per cent; Quebec, 36.2 per cent; Ontario, 30 per cent; the prairie provinces, 40 per cent; British Columbia, 34.5 per cent. Here again, there is some merit to Premier Bennett's thinking. If we were to distribute our wealth among the poor, 34.5 per cent of the unattached individuals in British Columbia would benefit from such a scheme.
I shall read some more figures which are also very revealing. They are found in a report prepared by Statistics Canada with regard to the percentage of dwellings in Canada having less than one room per person. Can the minister give us the assurance that redistribution of wealth will alleviate this problem? Dwellings in Canada having less than one room per person amounted to 22 per cent. For Manitoba the figure was 25 per cent. For Alberta, that wealthy province which is often considered to be one of those which pays the shot, the figure was 25 per cent. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) visited Alberta before the last election he said it had to pay the shot, but in fact rural Albertans are not enjoying the same high standard of living as some other regions. It is interesting to note that the Maritimes fared fairly well. The figures are: Prince Edward Island, 18 per cent; rural Nova Scotia, 18 per cent; rural New Brunswick, 25 per cent; rural Quebec, 29 per cent; rural Newfoundland, 29 per cent.
These figures indicate that all is not well in many regions which are considered wealthy and must pay the shot for many of the equalization and redistribution programs. They really do not enjoy the standard of living which they might. In fact, having studied these figures, as well as those relating to unemployment and wage levels in the various regions, I believe that people on the Prairies are prepared to, and do, work for less. This is not good because we are rewarding the less thrifty, and to some degree at least those who are not interested in working. This concept is wrong.
It is wrong to perpetuate this sort of situation. We should try through good legislation to reward the thrifty and encourage people to reach a high degree of fulfilment. A system that rewards effort and thrift will bring about a better Canada in which to live. This program is basically wrong. It will perpetuate poverty and welfare and encourage large families at the low income level where people are least able to educate their children in

order that they may take their place in the highly technological society in which we live.
I am disappointed that the minister has failed to give a breakdown of who will pay the increased tax and which regions will benefit so that we may know whether this program will alleviate poverty in our country. The minister could have devised a program much more in keeping with the needs of today's society.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of all the
stupid, idiotic, miserable and impossible bills introduced by this government, Bill C-170 must set a new highwater mark for bureaucratic bungling. Perhaps the bill should be entitled "an act to guarantee the establishment of bureaucracy" or "an act to drive ordinary taxpayers crazy." An ordinary person would have to lie awake at night for weeks to dream up anything as complicated. Even an ordinary nightmare would be a welcome relief after reading Bill C-170. This is a horrendous bill, Mr. Speaker. It fills the heart with despair that this government will ever abandon its penchant for symptom-treating. That is the fundamental objection: Bill C-170 is symptom-treating.
If the anti-poverty campaign of the past few years had been successful, this bill would not now be necessary. In fact, as was stated earlier in this debate, there is more poverty, relatively, today than when the anti-poverty campaign began a few years ago. There are much better ways to distribute income. The one that I would like to see adopted in this country is higher minimum wages. Frankly, I do not think there is any substitute for it.
During the past few years we have distorted our economy out of all reason until today we have people working in some parts of this country for $1.25 or $1.50 an hour while in other parts people with approximately the same level of education are earning $7, $8 or $9 an hour, plus fringe benefits. It is totally impossible for the person earning minimum wages or near minimum wages today to buy the products of those who are earning the higher wages. Something has to be done about this situation. In my opinion there is no better method than bringing minimum wages for employables up from the bottom. Not only must this be done but it must be done on an accelerated basis.
I am aware the minister might suggest that this is a provincial matter. I agree that it is in part a provincial matter. At the same time, there is no reason the federal government cannot get together with the provinces and work out ways of increasing minimum wages on an accelerated basis. If necessary, the federal government, with its tremendous fiscal leverage, can use moral suasion to get the provinces to take action.
Minimum wages is the best method of distributing income. It is the cheapest of all methods of doing so because there is no brokerage involved; there is no one to take a nickel or a dime off for administration since the payment is made directly to recipients. In my opinion there is no substitute for what is the most efficient, most
June 29, 1972

economic method of distributing income to employables, which is through minimum wages.
It has been argued that minimum wages raise costs and, therefore, the prices of marginal goods. This is true, of course. If one small shop or one small restaurant had to pay higher minimum wages than its competitors, it would be placed at a disadvantage. But if all similar establishments had to pay higher minimum wages the competitive position would remain intact.
If no other changes took place, the cost of the goods or services provided to the public would increase. But there is a related effect. Instead of collecting extra tax dollars necessary to finance some of these income redistribution schemes, the government could reduce taxes so as to compensate for, or at any rate largely offset, the effect of increased costs due to higher minimum wages. In these circumstances the effect of higher minimum wages would be mitigated. There would be no necessity for higher prices in most cases and in other cases only marginally higher prices would be necessary, not greater than those which would be required in any case as a result of higher tax levels.
So an increase in the minimum wage would not cost more, and it would probably cost less. It would cost less because it would not be necessary to collect money from the taxpayers on the one hand, to handle it at great cost through a large number of employees engaged in administration and then to redistribute it to many of the people who had paid it in the first place. In addition, it is socially more acceptable. There is something good about people getting their incomes in their own pay packets. There is something socially desirable about a system under which payments are made directly to recipients and subject to less probing by the bureaucracy; where there is less "big brother" interference in the lives of ordinary citizens.
One of the most regrettable developments in the last two decades has been the degree of insistent interference with the petty details of people's lives. Is it any wonder people are beginning to go right up the wall? The minister could take a lesson from what is happening in Sweden, where the level of bureaucratic interference is such that not only is efficiency falling off but people who were so proud of their democratic system until recently are now having serious doubts about it. The bureaucrats of this country are driving the little people crazy. It is a matter of sensitivity, a matter of humanity. The more interference there is in the details of people's lives, the more inhumane the system becomes.
Of particular interest is the provision here for adjustments to correspond to changes in the cost of living. This is another indication that the government has no serious intention of taking action to control inflation. This afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) told us that one more adjustment to compensate for inflationary rates was being made. Another occurs in the bill before us. We are bringing in more and more legislation containing provisions for adjustment to reflect increases in the cost of living.
Is this an admission that there is nothing we can do about inflation? Does it mean we have capitulated to this most insidious of all the threats to our economy, that we have given up all hope of being able to bring costs under
Family Income Security Plan
control, that the government has abdicated its responsibility and has no further plans to put before the Canadian people? It is evident that something has to be done. It is impossible to allow this erosion to take place at the present rate for many more years.
One must look ahead. With wage settlements following the present pattern, and on the basis of the existing rate of productivity in this country, by the end of the century milk will cost $1.65 a quart, a television set will cost $2,500 and a house that today costs $25,000 will cost $146,000. The worst aspect of these figures is that a great many ordinary, innocent people will be hurt in the process. So when we see the government once again coming forward with legislation and provisions which are nothing more than superficial symptom-treating, we begin to give up hope of any move toward more radical and positive alternatives.
I should like to recite what I think the positive alternatives should be. As far as employables are concerned, they should have access to jobs with decent wages. If the minister would do his mathematics he would find that a modest increase in the minimum wage would provide more relief for more Canadian families that are affected by the bill before us. And it would be a lot less complicated. The solution for employables, then, is jobs in such numbers that anyone who wants to work can work. There is no secrecy about how this can be done; all the orthodox economists know how to do it. It is being done in most countries of the western world-in Germany, Switzerland, and all the Nordic countries. It is being done in New Zealand and Japan. It is only in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and Italy that there is a high level of unemployment. And, of course, Canada has the worst record of all.
Wages for those who want to work should be high enough to enable them to look after all their basic requirements, that is to say, food, clothing, shelter and personal needs. Wages should be high enough to enable them to keep themselves and their families in reasonable dignity. This is an assurance of guaranteed annual work, which is an altogether different proposition from a guaranteed annual income, a direction in which the minister seems to be moving by the back door. I tell him that a guaranteed annual income is nothing more than institutionalized welfare. It is one of the most retrograde developments which could possibly be imagined. What it does is to establish as a matter of right those incomes that are sufficiently high as to be a disincentive to work for many people.
Whether the minister knows it or not, there are in Canada today tens of thousands of people who find themselves in the position where taking a job at or near minimum wages provides them with less cash disposable income than they can get from the welfare program. So guaranteed annual work, rather than guaranteed annual income, is the solution for employables.
For unemployables, of course, a guaranteed annual income is required. Once again, that guaranteed annual income for those who cannot work or are unable to work, for deserted mothers and so on, must be high enough to look after their basic necessities of life-food, clothing, shelter and personal requirements-so that they too do

June 29, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
not have to beg, so that they too do not have to look for aid from "big brother", so that they too do not have to look over their backs at weekends to see whether someone is watching them and seeing how they spend their time, whether they are doing a little moonlighting. In other words, we must restore a little dignity to human life by providing our unemployables with a guaranteed annual income that is sufficient for their basic needs.
We would then be able to use our tax laws to compensate people for the extra cost incurred in raising children. There is no reason why, with decent minimum wages for jobs which are available for those who want to work, our tax laws cannot be regulated in such a way that the extra income required to raise children is thus available to families with children.
One wonders, of course, whether a really progressive government that appreciates the necessity for going to zero population growth would want to encourage large families. In the event they decided that notwithstanding the consequences to the environment of this planet they wanted to encourage large families, or they just wanted to compensate people for the cost of the raising children who are already on this planet, there would be a better way to accomplish it than the proposals put forward in this bill. The government can still use the tax laws in order to provide the extra net income for a family's requirements.
In addition, as I have stated, it is necessary to protect the purchasing power of the ordinary people. We must control inflation; we cannot allow it to continue the way it is at the present time. I have stated over and over again that in my opinion there is no substitute for mandatory guidelines for wages and profits where monopoly power exists. If there is any other solution, I should like to know what it is; but to the best of my knowledge there is none.
Wages where monopoly power exists-which means where big unions exist-must be related to productivity. An increase in wages must be related to the average productivity increase in the whole economy. Then where giant companies are so big, so strong and powerful that they can regulate markets, their profits must be controlled in such a way that the benefits of the controlled wages are passed on to the consuming public. If that is done, then it is in fact possible to operate a free society in such a way that jobs are available for anyone who wants to work and, at the same time, the purchasing power of the Canadian economy is preserved and the savings of our senior citizens and others living on fixed incomes are kept intact.
I know of no other way to get to the position where prices are stable. It is possible to make our financial system work superbly and to provide jobs for all who want to work, at decent wages. It is possible to offer wages at a level high enough to look after family responsibilities. But this will require action quite different from that proposed in this House during recent weeks.
When one considers the common sense alternatives that are available, one wonders how Bill C-170 ever got through the cabinet. It is a terrible indictment of the cabinet system. Where is cabinet control of the bureaucracy? Where is cabinet control of its silly ministers? I hope the minister does not take offence at that remark, because

I know his heart is in the right place even if his legislation is every bit as bad as I have painted it. Certainly after reading the bill and the remarks the minister made in Quebec City recently, I must regretfully put the minister in that category. This is one of the problems with the present government. It has a lot of ministers who for one reason or another are guilty of what could be most generously described as fuzzy or furry thinking. And apparently the other ministers are unable to control them.
Where does the minister think that the money he needs will come from? He made a case today which I found very interesting: he said that it would not come from the middle class. I am wondering just where he thinks it will come from. He certainly is correct in saying that it will come from the middle class, because there is not enough money available from that source.
To illustrate this, recently I asked the parliamentary library to do an exercise for me to demonstrate what would happen if we taxed all incomes $20,000 and over at 100 per cent. The answer reveals that there would be about $250 million extra income, at least as I recall the figure. If this amount were distributed among the whole working force, each member of the working force would receive 1| cents an hour. If the level were reduced to $15,000 and all income above that was taxed at 100 per cent, you would have an additional income of about $530 million. Divided amongst the whole working force this would provide an extra three cents an hour. This is not the kind of aggregate that would gladden the hearts of the average working person in this country at the present time.
As I have suggested, Mr. Speaker, there is no way we can get the money required except by increasing production. The way to increase production is to get people off welfare and back into the work force. We must get people off unemployment insurance and back into the work force. If, as suggested earlier, by the leader of the New Democratic Party, we reduced the present level of unemployment from 6 per cent to 3 per cent, reducing the number out of work in this country from about 600,000 to 300,000, roughly $5 billion a year in real terms would be produced to enable us to do all the things that are required to make this country great.
This money can, of course, be used to eliminate poverty. It can be used to bring minimum incomes up to the point where people can breathe a little easier. It can be used to eliminate slums and wipe out the terrible shacks that exist in many parts of the country. Some of this money could be used to build houses for people and families who need them. Some of it could be used to construct an urban transportation system to enable people to travel around in some comfort, and thus some dignity would be restored to urban living. Some of it could be used for the development of industries and resources in Canada-this would be Canadian capital-if only our tax laws encouraged savings, as opposed to the kind of laws passed recently by this Parliament which had the opposite, negative effect.
If the economic management of this country was worth anything, we would have available extra resources to the tune of $4 billion or $5 billion annually over and above natural growth. This could be used to eliminate poverty, slums, to build houses, to construct an urban transporta-
June 29, 1972

tion system and to develop our resources. In other words, it would enable us to do those things which Canadians want done. That is the method we should adopt. That is the direction we should take, rather than taking more income out of the present pot and passing it to people who in many cases have no incentive to get back into the work force.
The present policy is retrogressive both economically and socially. It is retrogressive economically in the sense that every person who is discouraged from participating in the work force means less productivity, and thus we are unable to do all those things which remain to be done. It is retrogressive socially because most people are happier when they are working, when they have something productive and worth while to do and feel important. They are happier if they feel they are part of the process and Eire needed and wanted. It is socially more desirable to have people working than having a welfare system which discourages their working. Of course this happens, and I can give the minister many individual cases if he is interested in having them.
We are already reaching the point of diminishing returns and to push tax rates higher would be another folly. In the last two weeks I have talked to a number of individuals who already have refused to work overtime. By the time the government takes its cut, they say it is not worth while. One would expect that this would apply to a number of people in the professions, and it does. Now it has come down to a level which I would call the average working level.
Recently I was involved in a television interview and the CBC technician behind the camera came over afterward and said he refused to work any more overtime. He was a single man and the tax rates are so high that he feels there is no point working overtime; it was not worth while. A week ago Saturday I attended a garden party in my riding at a home for senior citizens, and the chief nurse said the same thing. She said she would no longer work overtime bec'ause there was no percentage in it for her. She said she was working that day and would take time off. She would not work overtime because the taxes she had to pay to the government of Canada and to other levels of government were so high it was not worth while; she was going to take time off instead.
We have reached the point of diminishing returns, and there is no place from which the extra tax money required for these new measures can come unless we put back to work people who are presently unemployed and who in most cases would welcome a chance to go to work if wages were high enough to enable them to keep themselves. You cannot blame somebody for not going to work when he can make 20 per cent or 30 per cent more by staying home than by re-entering the work force.
One might also ask where the Liberal backbenchers were when this bill was being presented. Did they object to it in caucus? I know what some of them think by listening to them over here, ministers and backbenchers alike. They think this is a very bad bill. Most of them do not want to fight an election on it and hope it will not go through in the next two days, yet they let it through
Family Income Security Plan
caucus and they come in and rubberstamp it. Are they as incapable of exercising independent thought as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said they were when he was writing in "Cite Libre" some years ago? We have a chance to find out in the course of the next two days.
I suppose one might ask the official opposition if this is not an opportunity for them. Surely they do not want something as complicated as this bill to pass the House. Surely if they are serious about forming a government later this year they would not want to foreclose their opportunity by allowing this bill to pass at this time. Surely they could come up with something more ingenious than this bill. Surely they have some ideas of their own they would like to put forward after the election. If they are serious and really believe there is any possibility of forming a government, then to demonstrate that belief they should hold up this bill so it does not pass and clear the deck for action with measures of a more ingenious and fundamental character when the next Parliament is called later this year. That is what I would recommend.
I would recommend that all people who believe the time for symptom-treating has come to an end, who believe we must get back to fundamentals and start curing diseases rather than putting band-aid on top of band-aid, should vote against this bill, stop it in its tracks. Then perhaps at the next Parliament of Canada someone will come up with a fundamental measure that will enable people of this country who want to work, to work for wages high enough to keep themselves and their families in decency and at the same time make a contribution to both the economic and social welfare of this great nation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill C-170 is really a debate in respect of a basic principle. I recognize that the waters have been muddied a good deal and we have got away from serious discussion of the principle that I believe should be central to this debate, but the principle is still there. It is because in our view that principle is a very important one both now and in the future that we still think the government should not press Parliament to pass this legislation at this time.
As I suggested yesterday when we were at the committee stage, I strongly believe this bill should be taken back to the drawing boards, and I still make that plea to the minister as earnestly as I can. I said there is a principle at stake in this bill. That principle, as I see it, is simply this: Are we going to treat people in Canada as people, or are we going to treat them as pawns in an economic mess? When any government provides assistance to its people, whether it is called welfare, allowances or what-have-you, because they are poor, and when any government bases its social programs on poverty it is violating the principle that people have rights because they are people.
I believe in the redistribution of wealth. I do not think it is yet within the capacity of mankind to devise an economic system which will automatically distribute the wealth we produce on the basis of equality, yet I think that a civilization which is civilized ought to aim at equality, and I favour the redistribution of wealth being done through progressive taxation and the distribution of allowances to people to enable them to enjoy an adequate standard of living. I want those allowances to go to

June 29, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
people, old age citizens, mothers, children and what-have-you, not because certain of those people are poor but because they are people and have the right to share in the wealth this country produces.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) is sitting there ready to say he has heard this speech from me ten, fifty or a thousand times, but it is still true that over the years we have made some progress in this Parliament. The day came when we took away from our older people the stigma that was attached to them when pensions were given only if they declared their absolute poverty. That day came when we established old age security on a universal basis. We had enough years of experience with old age security on a universal basis to be able to compare that experience with what had gone on before. I am prepared to assert and reassert that we gave to many senior citizens in those years a dignity that we denied our older people in earlier years.
We gave to Louis St. Laurent when he became 70, we gave to other politicians, we gave to professionals, to working people and so-called poor people the same basic pension. We accorded a dignity to old age because we gave it to Canadians over a certain age, not because they were poor but because they were Canadians of that age. We did not ask them to declare their poverty in order to receive that pension. No matter how much the Minister of National Health and Welfare wants to chide me about making this speech times without number, and no matter how uncomfortable he feels because I assert this is one good thing a Liberal government once did, it is a fact it was a piece of legislation that was good. The thing that was good about it was that it accepted the basic principle that people should be treated by the economy of the country-and after all, it is the government which has control of it-not in terms of their wealth or poverty but in terms of their being people.
I say to you, sir, that we did the same thing in 1944 in respect of family allowances. The amount of money that was provided was very small, and I do not want to subscribe to all the things Mr. Mackenzie King said about the humble poor, the working poor, and so on, when he was putting this legislation through; but the basic principle of that legislation was good. We said we were going to provide an amount of money for the children of this country because they were the children of this country. We attached no means test to it. It was a good piece of legislation.
However, this government headed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), a latecomer to the Liberal party who decided that the Liberals who went before him did not know what they were talking about, decided that the progress we made toward universality, toward the payment of pensions and allowances to people, not as welfare or as handouts because they were poor but as their share of the wealth that was being produced, was wrong. The cabinet ministers over there have now decided that was wrong. I submit to them that they have not thought the matter through and that they are turning back the clock of history so far as Canada is concerned.

Just as it was wrong to attach a means, a needs or an income test to a portion of the old age pension, so it is wrong in principle to attach a means or a needs or income test to the family allowance. I urge as strongly as I can that the minister, who along with my leader I think has a good heart, not have it on his record that in his younger years, instead of helping to achieve progress in this country he turned the clock backward and returned to the practice of payment of allowances to children on the basis of poverty.

speechtext:
I do not know what that has to do with it but I suppose the point is well taken, that it is the Prime Minister who made this decision and that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is just carrying out the decision the Prime Minister made. Now they have decided that Mackenzie King, Louis St. Laurent and Lester Pearson did not know what they were talking about when they tried to establish and reinforce the principle of universality.
I realize I am repeating myself, but to me this is terribly important. I think we are talking about the most important aspect of social policy that this Parliament ever considers. When we give money to people because they are poor and make them declare their poverty, we keep them in that poverty. One of the things I do not like about this FISP legislation, if it goes through, is that I think just as welfare has produced generations which are on welfare because the former generation was, so we will divide this country into the haves and have-nots and many of the have-nots are families with children who will receive the FISP benefit because they have met a poverty test, and those children will grow up to become the parents of families which will do the same thing. Do we not want to bring a halt to this?
In all our discussions about national unity we hear a great deal about language and race. If there is to be national unity, it must be in economic terms. We must move in the direction of economic equality among our people. We will not do this by the method of saying to people that they will receive the allowances they are entitled to, not because they are Canadians but because they declare their poverty.
This morning when the Minister of National Health and Welfare was making that interesting speech, the purpose of which is obscure, he had quite a bit to say about our charge that this legislation stigmatizes those who will receive these FISP cheques. He is quite justified in saying that quite a bit was said over here about the comer grocery store man knowing the position of certain families when he would cash the cheques, and so on. Because things like that were mentioned over here I do not blame him for trying to answer them.
However, the minister missed the main way in which this legislation will stigmatize and dehumanize people. It is very simple. We now have a family allowance program for which people qualify because they have children of certain ages; that is all there is to it. But under the new legislation the only way one can receive a benefit under FISP is by declaring his poverty. I do not want Canadians to be forced by legislation to declare their poverty, or for them to start a tradition in which their children and their
June 29, 1972

children's children will do the same thing. I want to move in the direction of economic equality. We will get there a lot faster with universal programs than we ever would with the kind of legislation the minister now has placed before us.
As I say, there is a lot of talk about the need for Canadian unity. We have to get together among the provinces, the provinces have to get together with the federal government and both have to get together with the language groups, and so on. I agree on the need for Canadian unity, but I insist there will not be real unity until there is an equal opportunity among all people in this country to enjoy a decent standard of living.
The hon. member who spoke just before me seemed worried about the guaranteed income and people having the right to welfare. I think he put it this way. If I am misquoting him, I trust he will forgive me. It seems to me what is wrong in his thinking is his failure to realize that there are already things to which people have a right. People have a right to live. People have a right to use the roads and highways and the postal service. People have the right to be defended and protected. They have the right to education. We say people have a right to decent housing, and they also have the right to enough money to be able to enjoy a decent standard of living. We believe that right should no more depend on whether or not they are lucky enough to get remunerative employment than the right to an education should depend on whether they were born in a poor or a wealthy home. It is because we believe that the redistribution of wealth should be done on the basis of right that we favour allowances being given on a universal basis rather than as welfare payments being handed out on a basis of one's declaration of poverty.
So I say that we are discussing today one of the most important matters of principle that we ever discuss in this House of Commons. The whole issue has been with us for a long time. Among the things that I have read fairly often is the report of the Liberal convention of 1919 when they were concerned about unemployment, old age and sickness and pledged themselves to do something about those difficulties. It took them a long while to sort out their thinking. But I have to say for the Liberals that even though it may have taken prodding from this side of the House to make them do it, they came to the point when they realized that these problems were not to be solved by welfare handout programs but, rather, by universal allowances or by insurance programs.
I think the travail that the Liberal party went through for a few decades to come to this position was worth it. The trouble is now-and it is a tragedy for Canada-that the Liberal government is headed by a Prime Minister who thinks he knows better than all the Liberals who went before him, so he has handed out the dictum that the way the other Liberals did it is not the right way. So now they foreswear the principle of universality, the very principle that led this Parliament to bring in good social legislation.
I believe it is most unfortunate that this has happened to the Liberal party. If it had happened only to the Liberal
Family Income Security Plan
party it might not be so bad, but because the Liberal party is in power it is happening to the country as a whole. I see this piece of legislation, if it goes on the statute books, as an unfortunate one, not just for the mess that I will talk about in a few minutes but because I think it turns back the clock; it increases the sense of division in this country; it divides us into haves and have-nots; it perpetuates living on handouts, on welfare, on means tests or income test programs instead of enjoying one's share of the wealth that we produce because we are people, because we are Canadians and because we are part of this great country.
If we cannot persuade the government under the present Prime Minister to realize the mistake that it is making, I hope that at least by debating this measure, as now seems likely in view of the speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, we may yet give the government the summer to think it all over.
I said a moment ago that I would say something about the mess that this legislation will create. There is no doubt about that. It is true that some of the many difficulties that the new Unemployment Insurance Act created have lessened, but they have not gone. We still have cases of persons over 65 or over 70 years of age having received unemployment insurance benefits being told a few months later that they have to return the $200 or $300 they received. One can imagine the tragedies that this kind of thing produces.
We still have people not receiving the benefits to which they are entitled or having to go through all sorts of rigmarole. Why? Because a relatively understandable Unemployment Insurance Act was replaced by one that had in it so many complications that it is just not working. The troubles that the computer had with the Unemployment Insurance Act are minor compared to the troubles the computer will have with this act. The minister and his officials have had to admit from time to time that it will take longer and longer to get this legislation into effect.
Originally, there was a bill under which payments were to have been made last month, in May, 1972. Now we have a bill the intention of which was that the payments would be made in September or October of 1972. That has been delayed to December and then to January. Yesterday the minister admitted that very probably the payments under the new legislation will not be made, even if the bill passes now, until next summer, the summer of 1973. I suggest to you, Sir, that if it will take that long to get it started, it is an indication of the length of time that will be needed to sort out the complications and the messes that will arise under this legislation.
It has been said many times that the amount that you get will have to be readjusted time and time again because people do not live lives under static conditions. The average family finds its income going up or down, finds the number of children increasing or decreasing and their ages changing. There are cases where people go on unemployment insurance and then go back to work again, or have periods when they do not get either, so that the amount of income a person will have in a year is an unknown quantity at the beginning of the year and in some cases is unknown at the end of the year. All these

June 29, 1972
Family Income Security Plan things can determine the amount that each family will get under FISP.
The result of all this, as I say, is that there will be a complicated mess, and in addition to the delays and changes that will take place there will be the fear that thousands of mothers and families will have, that they may be saying the wrong thing, that they may be making a mistake, that they may have failed to report something which they should have reported. The result will be that they will put themselves in danger of having to pay moneys back or face prosecution.
Compare all that with the simple system we have had since 1944 under which all of these other economic factors did not matter at all. I submit that these complications make this bill one that no sensible group of people, such as I hope we have in the House of Commons, should accept. I disagree with a good deal that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) said in the speech he made this afternoon, although I understand some of what he said and agree with some of it. But what interested me most was his reflection, as one who sits to Your Honour's right, of the kind of talking that is going on in the Liberal party. He is not of them any more, but he is over there with them and he made it clear to us that there are many of them, ministers and backbenchers alike, who hope this legislation will not go through.
As a matter of fact, this morning when the Minister of National Health and Welfare made that very provocative speech I wondered if that was his purpose. Was he trying to provoke more speeches in this debate so that the bill would not get through today or tomorrow?

I do not think that the minister, whom I knew under other circumstances when he was a private member sitting on the opposition side of the House, and when he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of national health and welfare during the Canada Pension Plan days, is the person whom I knew in those days. I do not think he believes in the principle which the Prime Minister has told him must be enshrined in this legislation. For all these reasons, and in particular because of the complicated mess that this legislation will produce, we think it should not be passed today or tomorrow.
In passing I would like to make reference to another awkward situation that is likely to develop. If my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Macln-nis), gets the floor in this debate she will enlarge upon it because it is a matter that she raised when the bill was before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. But in case she is delayed in joining the debate, she has asked me if I would mention it now. As the minister knows, my colleague asked questions in the committee about the possibility of the FISP benefits being

treated as income for purposes of welfare payments in some of the provinces. In particular, she asked whether any steps would be taken to make sure that this would not happen. This was dealt with in the committee on May 24, 1972. The record of that discussion is on pages 9:20 and 9:21. I will not take the time to read what is said there, but I would point out that the minister simply expressed the hope that they would not do it but he was not able to give an assurance. He insisted that it was not the job of the federal government to require provinces to sign an agreement in this respect.
I have in my hand a letter which the national anti-poverty organization of Alberta sent to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, with a carbon copy to all Alberta members as well as to other interested members, in which it is pointed out that in Alberta the present family allowance payments are not regarded as income for the purposes of welfare, but there is every indication that in that province family income security benefits, mainly because they will be larger, in some cases will be counted as income for the purposes of welfare payments. The result could well be a smaller total cash flow to individual families.
My colleague tells me that the same thing is likely to happen in British Columbia. I say to the minister that the provinces which provide welfare payments do so on the basis of the Canada Assistance Plan, which is funded 50 per cent by the federal government, and I see no reason why the government could not find a way to make sure that payments made under FISP are not counted as income and therefore deducted from the welfare payments made in the provinces.
I hope my colleague will be able to get into this debate at some point and develop this matter. I mention it here as one complication that is bound to develop with this kind of legislation. Indeed, complications are bound to develop with respect to the whole nature of this program, which is the welfare program that the hon. member for Trinity does not like. I quite agree with him in his opposition to welfare. Where I disagree with him is in his opposition to a guaranteed income, his opposition to redistributing wealth with the aim of providing an adequate and decent standard of living for all our people.

-that will really redistribute wealth and bring something approaching equality to this country. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who has made a number of interjections which I have not stopped to listen to, says there is no way for that to work. Mr. Speaker, let it be on the record that I, too, do not believe it is possible to devise an economic system that will distribute income and wealth equally to all citizens. I think it is the job of government to step in and do that, because people are people no matter where they were born.
I suspect that many of us in this chamber were born under conditions of poverty. I am not going to recite my own case, for there are many others in this House who could do likewise. A number of us have been able to break through the barrier, to get into a little better climate of life; but that number is few. What I do not like is that so many people are confined to the same level, the same stratum of society in which their parents lived.
I think that as we go on with these kinds of payments, based on poverty, that is what we perpetuate. I do not want to perpetuate it. I want to work by every means we can, under federal and provincial legislation, to a greater redistribution of the wealth of this country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we want to see an increase in the payments of what we have known since 1944 as family allowances. We welcome the proposal in this bill that instead of paying $6, $8 and $10 at various ages, we pay $15 and $20.1 would be quite happy to see those amounts made larger. I will not waste any time on the question of where the money would come from, because my leader the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) completely demolished the arguments made by the minister this morning in that respect.
As a matter of fact, I have spent my whole adult life listening to Liberals, from Charlie Dunning on down, saying that we cannot find the money to do this or that, yet I have seen Liberal governments find the money when they have been forced into doing things. We urge that the payments stipulated in this bill be made on a universal basis. We think that the tax structure should be revamped so that those in the upper brackets will pay them back.
I am quite prepared to accept what the Canadian Council on Social Development has sometimes called an arrangement whereby they are clawed back, even in some cases up to 100 per cent. The minister asked whether we want a system whereby we give the money to a wife and then make the husband pay it back. Most husbands are used to that. That is the way we have been doing it under the Family Allowances Act; the money has been going to the wife, to the mother. We think that should continue to be the case, but with an income tax system that would take it back from those in the upper brackets.
If any individuals wished not to apply, then they would not have to apply. I am not worried about wealthy people having to declare their wealth for the payment of income tax, but I am annoyed that poor people have to declare their poverty in order to get what is their right. That is why my colleagues and I feel strongly that this legislation should not be put through in its present form, but that it either should be taken back to the drawing board by the government or referred back to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs so that we can keep
Family Income Security Plan
in it the higher amounts of $15 and $20 but put out of it the means, or needs, or income test provisions that are now in it. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for V ancouver-Kingsway:
That Bill C-170 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs for the purpose of reconsidering the portions of clause 6 and of such other clauses that impose a means or income test for the receipt of benefits under the said bill.

Not according to what I hear; there are great differences of opinion between those hon. members. The minister in his speech this morning mentioned ideas which come within the widest parameters. In putting a dollar figure against these ideas, he conveniently forgot the net cost to government that this program involves. Of course, he may have considered the matter on a gross cost basis. The various methods of redistribution, say the old age pension, unemployment insurance and other programs, come within the purview of income tax, and this is where I differ from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I agree that the entitlement to benefits for children should be determined on a universal basis. However, if we are to achieve the aims of this bill, surely the simplest way would be by putting family allowances under the Income Tax Act. Let them be subject to income tax. We do this with old age security. At one time I thought the NDP would adopt that position. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has not spoken about this, so I do not know whether he has abandoned the idea that family allowances ought to be subject to income tax. Entitlement to benefit ought to vary according to ability to pay. In that way, low income people and those with large numbers of children would obtain greater entitlement. This, I put to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members is the thrust and purpose of the bill.
What will we do under this bill? We shall create an administrative monster. We shall ask every parent, living singly or otherwise, to estimate family income. On the basis of that estimate the allowance will be paid. There is no guarantee that the mother will work and earn that income. If she is a part-time employee she may not earn as much as she estimated, or she may earn more. If she does earn more, at the end of the year money must be repaid to the state; an adjustment must be made. If you think there will be no opportunity for those who desire to fiddle, think again. Right at that point there will be an open invitation to fiddle.
My second point is that there will be difficulty, as there is with unemployment insurance benefits, in the recovery of overpayments.

As there are no private bills listed on the order paper, the House will proceed immediately to the consideration of notices of motions for the production of papers.

That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the interim report made in March, 1968, by Dr. A. Vennema, director of Canadian medical aid in Vietnam in 1967-68 and for copies of any subsequent correspondence between him and the Department of External Affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, two years ago I placed on the order paper a request for the production of papers connected with the report of Dr. A. Vennema. At that time the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) I believe had placed a similar request on the order paper. On March 8 of this year the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Isabelle) replied to my request in the following words:
Mr. Speaker, all experts such as Dr. Vennema, who perform a particular service under contract to the Canadian International Development Agency, submit reports on their respective projects as a matter of routine. These reports and other correspondence are submitted on the understanding that they will be treated as confidential and privileged documents. If these experts felt that such documents could be made public they would be reticent about making meaningful comments that would help in the effective implementation of Canada's aid program. For these reasons I ask, with regret, that the hon. member withdraw her motion.
This I refuse to do for reasons which I shall make evident. Who is Dr. Alje Vennema, whose report I requested? Dr. Vennema, according to the biography accompanying his article in "Canadian Commentator" published in Toronto, was head of Canadian medical services in South Viet Nam from 1964 to 1968. He was later awarded the
June 29, 1972

medal of the Order of Canada for his services in that capacity. Following his work in South Viet Nam he submitted a report to the government. It is this report that I have been unable to get. His report has been buried in the vaults of the Department of External Affairs. In other words, he was given a medal and told to be quiet.
What is contained in the report we do not know exactly, but we have a fair idea because of the article which he wrote for "Canadian Commentator" last summer. I quote from this article:
Canada was supposed to be neutral and objective. We could have drawn the attention of the Americans to the catastrophe they had unleashed upon the Vietnamese by telling them: "What you are doing is not only disastrous, it's tragic, it's godawful and you ought to stop it."
But we always tried to placate the Americans in almost everything. The Canadian delegation to the ICC was in essence an extension of the U.S. State Department. If there was an important decision in an area that might hurt the Americans, the Canadians would make sure it wasn't published.
Most of the Canadians with the ICC felt they were doing the right thing. Many shared the American opinion that there was a place for the Americans in Viet Nam, fighting Communism and infiltration from the north. Some thought it was a useless situation to be in; others, that the Canadian component of the ICC existed to further the affairs of the West, as the Poles represented the East and there were those who felt anything being done was the right thing to stem the tide of Communism. Yet we were in a unique position to tell the Americans: "Look, what's going on here is a tragedy".
I went to South Viet Nam to join the American Dr. Tom Dooley's medical mission and moved to the Canadian mission in 1964. Under the terms on which Canadian medical aid was extended to Viet Nam in 1954 we were supposed to deal with both North and South Viet Nam through a liaison committee. But we didn't really want to give aid to the North and we never offered it. We didn't deal through the liaison committee but through an exchange of notes with the South Vietnamese government, which was de facto recognition of that government. Every time there was a coup and the government changed we exchanged notes but we never had a project agreement although we spent more than three million dollars.
Our services were not directly concerned with the war as we were dealing with tuberculosis and nutrition and so on in the TB hospital we built in Quang Ngai.
But I handled 20-30 napalm bomb casualties in the hospital. When a Toronto Star reporter wrote this the ICC delegation got cables from Ottawa saying "Better talk to Vennema about this. This type of thing should not be said. The U.S. government says there are no napalm cases in this province."
In 1967-68 I first told about the American use of gas. The Canadian delegate, Ormond Dier, called me in and said "What's this?" I said I had handled people affected by gas-likely CS or CN. He said the delegation was upset that this had been put out and advised me to keep quiet.
Don't forget, this man was later awarded the Order of Canada. He is not a man who can be lightly brushed aside.
Blair Seaborn, the ICC delegate who carried U.S. messages to Hanoi was, I thought, a very reasonable man who had a good grasp of the situation, but he was just a go-between and he personally had no decision or say-so in anything. The decisions were made between Ottawa and Washington-
I left the hospital in 1968. It was taken over by the South-Viet-namese army paramilitary forces who used it as a firing base- what the hell is the use of making a hospital and having it used as a firing base? I suggested to Ormond Dier that he withdraw all his voluntary medical personnel because they were risking their lives. Secondly, I said, by providing medical aid what you are really doing is prolonging the conflict. South-Vietnamese doctors and nurses were never much interested in their own people and the
Vennema Report on Viet Nam War
medical services in the country were being rendered by foreign personnel.
Dier's response was that we must have Canadians at Quang Ngai because it was very important for Canada to be in Viet Nam. Canadians had died for Canada before, he said. I asked if it's that important why don't you send a civil servant there from the department of external affairs who can just sit there and wave a flag? But he put a lot of things into perspective for me. What was important in Viet Nam was Canadian representation-to show we were there. Again, to placate the Americans. There was nothing we could do in Viet Nam without the Americans. We depended on them for transportation, often for food, for everything.
This article was written by the man whose report I am trying to obtain. This is some indication of the tenor of the report and why we cannot get it. This man has refused to be shut up by the receipt of the Order of Canada. His four years in the South Viet Nam hell performing medical service ought to be given respect by making his opinions and report available to the representatives of this country. We do not know exactly what is contained in his report but I think this article indicates what is likely to be there.
The remarks of the parliamentary secretary about meaningful comments that would help in the effective implementation of Canada's aid program take on a different meaning. The parliamentary secretary indicated that reports such as this can be released only if they are helpful to Canada's aid program. What aid program? Canada's aid program to the Vietnamese, or Canada's aid to the American attempt to wipe them out? All through the piece, all through this costly, dragged-out war Canada has been the silent partner in the murder of the Vietnamese people. True, we have had a hospital there to bind the wounds and care for the sick, but our country, through defence sharing agreements, has helped to supply the means of killing and mutilating the people and despoiling and destroying their country.
Dr. Vennema's former assistant in the Canadian antituberculosis hospital at Quang Ngai, Claire Culhane, has written a description of the dreadful and unbearable horrors she witnessed daily in the course of her nursing work there. Her feeling of the hypocritical futility of the whole Canadian exercise of caring for the victims while helping to cause the casualties is summed up in her description of the case of one young patient. She writes:
In the soft tissue ward I had been nursing a youngster whose entire body was one big open wound, but it was healing. Gradually, after three months of careful treatment he was beginning to be able to romp around the ward, quite naked as he could not bear to have anything touch his raw flesh. One morning I came in to find he had been discharged home. The utter futility of our TLC (tender-loving-care) program filled me with despair. If he didn't get bombed or blown up on the way home (two provinces distant)-if there was a home and a family still there-with no further treatment and only dirt and dust to play in, he would surely become infected and die in no time at all. All we had been doing for three months was treating a doomed child. But what degree of difference was the prospect for any of the other patients as soon as they left the hospital? Every procedure was just an exercise in futility and could not have been made more vivid than at that moment.
That is Claire Culhane who went through the hell over there at that period of time. Mr. Speaker, I think it is time we began to realize we are living in a single world and that all these imperialisms and frontiers are dangerous;
