The motion we are considering has been on the order paper for a long time and Dr. Vennema's report has been in the hands of the government for a much longer time. The war which was described by the former Secretary General of the United Nations, U Thant, as "this monstrous war" still goes on. Canada's "Pentagon Papers" should be released. The people have a right to the facts. They paid for the preparation of the report. They sent Dr. Vennema over there, and no matter what they thought of his political opinions the government has recognized his services by awarding him the Order of Canada.
The very least we should do in this instance is to air the facts in the way the American facts have been coming out and allow the people of this country to know the truth of Canada's role in the war in Viet Nam. It is no longer good enough to say, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did when questioned about the $300 million worth of military equipment being sold to the United States by Canada and which found its way to Viet Nam, "The choice is between $300 million sales or clean hands and empty bellies." I believe the Prime Minister was exceedingly wide of the mark: that is not the choice. As the Americans are learning, the choice is not between clean hands and empty bellies, but between using the equipment and technology they possess for the purposes of war, killing, destroying, mutilating and ruining the environment, and turning that technological know-how and skill to the purposes of peace. That is the choice in front of us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What about the aid coming from the Russians?

I don't care what the Russians, the Chinese or anybody else are doing. That is not germane. I am talking about Canada. Canada is our backyard and we should be cleaning it up before we go around finding out what anybody else is doing. This is the place we can control and that is what we should be doing. As a first step we should not be afraid of getting at the truth. If Canada has been an accomplice in this matter and still is, I think it is time the Canadian people were made aware of it. If Dr. Vennema's report contains facts and figures about what he has been doing in Viet Nam, and deals with what he saw in addition to his medical work, we deserve to hear those facts. Let us not forget that Dr. Vennema was regarded highly enough by this country to be awarded the Order of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For the work he has done there.

All right, for the work he has done there. But not only for the work he has done, which is only part of the thinking that merited the award. Certainly we should not censor Dr. Vennema's report. The government has no right to censor that report or to black it out entirely. The people of this country have a right to be given the facts. This is the reason several of us in the House have hung on doggedly, despite the amount of time which has gone by since the motion was placed on the order paper and despite the fact that Dr. Vennema must have long ago given up hope of getting this matter brought out into the public gaze. Claire Culhane has also

worked very hard in this regard, as have a great many others, protesting that it is not too late to bring out these facts. It is never too late to bring out the truth into the light of day for people to see.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this opportunity to speak in connection with this motion for the production of papers. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) said a few moments ago, the issue involved here is not a new one. It is tragic that it is still a contemporary issue in that the conflict in Viet Nam continues, as does the complicity of Canada in that conflict. It is disturbing, especially when one considers the wanton destruction of life and environment in that tragic little land of Viet Nam.
I have been particularly concerned with the lack of forthrightness of the government, not only in reference to Dr. Alje Vennema, with whom I have had an opportunity to talk from time to time, but with reference to a whole host of people many of whom have been sent to Viet Nam over the years and who have come back to Canada with serious reports only to have the greater part of them swept under the rug.
It is interesting when we recall, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has pointed out, the high regard in which Dr. Alje Vennema is held in this country and the award he has received. I could mention, in addition, people such as Dr. Gustav Gingras who recently received an award from, I believe, the Royal Bank of Canada of $50,000 for his great work in rehabilitation. I think members on both sides of the House will remember that Dr. Gingras was involved in the examination of a possible rehabilitation program under which children were to be brought from Viet Nam to this country, as well as with rehabilitation work with children in Viet Nam. Again, he was most critical of the posture and performance of the Canadian government toward that country. It is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that anyone who attempts to deal with the humanitarian issues which are at stake in Viet Nam immediately becomes concerned about the role played by the Canadian government in that conflict.
It was much more comfortable for the government and for Canadians generally to be in support of the role of Canada in Viet Nam while there was still widespread support for the United States interest and involvement in the conflict. However, since the decline of American support for its own involvement in that war, the revelations which have been made with regard to the atrocities committed and the real political issues at stake in that country have impressed both young and old alike with the folly and, of course, the tragedy of the war. The tragedy in the first instance, of course, involves the people of Viet Nam themselves. The tragedy for the United States, and the tragedy for Canada, lies in allowing itself the foolishness of getting involved in that conflict and for believing it had interests at stake great enough to encourage the destruction of a people and of a land.
The United States has not yet extricated itself from that war. There is a widespread belief both here and in the United States that this will happen. But at some time there will need to be an accounting taken, not only by the Americans of what they have lost and suffered in the conflict but of Canada's own role. It will not be a happy
June 29, 1972

one. When the story can be fully told by Dr. Gingras, Dr. Vennema, Claire Culhane and the secret reports of the International Control Commission, as well as all the other documents and papers which the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway suggested are secreted away in some vault, I have a deep-seated belief that Canadians will be sorely ashamed.
It is an easy thing to say. It has become increasingly obvious that we have willingly consented to a good deal of the United States military intervention in Viet Nam and that our aid projects as such have been, as I think has been suggested, 50 per cent humanitarian and 50 per cent political. Much of what has been declared as aid has of necessity been tinged politically because we have offered cover, protection and assistance to the military of South Viet Nam and of the United States.
We have proclaimed that we are, in one sense, neutral. But we have not been neutral. It is a well documented fact that we have supplied hundreds of millions of dollars worth of destructive materials which have been used to cause injury and death in South Viet Nam. Yet we have attempted to provide some kind of humanitarian program under the umbrella of the South Vietnamese military regime and the United States military government. This has never been clearly stated by any prime minister or minister of the government, but it cannot be denied for it would not be true to deny it. We have given no official recognition to the regimes of either Hanoi or Saigon, yet we have been a willing ally in terms of our activities with the Saigon regime. We have, of course, had no contact, apart from what limited contact has been available through the ICC, with the Hanoi regime.
There are two fundamental issues at stake this afternoon. One issue is Canada's real role in Viet Nam both in terms of military hardware and in terms of aid and humanitarian programs. There has been no tragedy greater for North America during the last decade than its involvement in Viet Nam. To the degree that we have encouraged or assisted in that conflict and extended it, we must admit that in one sense we have been duped and in another sense more than duped. Perhaps we have been willing accomplices-mistakenly, perhaps-with regard to the real issues in this conflict.
It has been stated very clearly by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that there is a good deal to know about Canada's aid program in Viet Nam. For the last four sessions, with the exception of the present brief session, I have continued to have on the order paper a notice for production of papers asking for the documents relating to Mrs. Claire Culhane. Mrs. Culhane is a rather well known individual in this country for she has demonstrated unceasingly against Canadian involvement in Viet Nam. She has created something of a reputation for herself because of her single-mindedness on this issue.
What she has tried to bring forward in every possible way in conversations with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as well as through repeated letters to ministers and members of the House, is the full round of reports that she herself has made. On an earlier occasion when I attempted to obtain these reports and documents which
Vennema Report on Viet Nam War
she has filed as CIDA adviser, I was told by the officials of the minister's department that if the documents were made public they would very likely be libellous.
What I was asking for were documents that Mrs. Culhane had herself submitted. I assume that if they were libellous, Mrs. Culhane would have to accept responsibility for them, and it has always been my impression that this is what she was prepared to do. Yet the government has been most reluctant to provide the full facts and background information respecting her reports and other reports which have been filed over that period. I submit it is important that the Canadian people know what in fact has been the role of the Canadian government in regard to its aid programs in this terrible conflict. If it is the wish of this particular government not to make these records available, then it is paramount that some future government do so in the interests of the Canadian people.
The second issue at stake here is directly related to this whole business of production of papers. Yesterday afternoon I was, quite frankly, very tempted to rise on a point of order immediately following the point of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when consent to a motion for production of papers was refused to the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom). I think in Hansard for yesterday afternoon we have a classic record of the inability of this House to deal effectively with the production of papers. As reported at page 3596, the following motion No. 48 put on the order paper by the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville was moved:
That an order of the House do issue for copies of all contracts dealing with publicity and/or information entered into by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in the fiscal years 1970-71 and 1971-72.
That notice of motion for production of papers was agreed to. Then in the very next instance, as recorded on the next page, notice of motion No. 46, again standing in the name of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, was moved, asking as follows:
That an order of the House do issue for copies of all contracts deaing with publicity and/or information entered into by the Department of National Health and Welfare in the fiscal years 1970-71 and 1971-72.
The parliamentary secretary replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, we cannot accede to the request of the hon. member because a contract is a confidential document between the individual and his employer.
What kind of situation do we have, Mr. Speaker, when in one instance one parliamentary secretary says the motion is perfectly acceptable and that the government is prepared to respond by tabling papers and documents, and the very next moment another parliamentary secretary says it would not be proper for such a motion to be accepted1? I think this illustrates that at the present time the only rules governing production of papers in this House can be very simply stated as follows: Yes we want to do it, no we don't.
Quite frankly, Sir, I think in your capacity as senior officer of the House a special responsibility falls upon you, and particularly on those concerned with the procedures used in this place, to scrutinize very carefully what the House adopts as its customary practice in regard to

June 29, 1972
Vennema Report on Viet Nam War the tabling of documents. It is a matter of increasing concern not only to Members of Parliament but to the general public that larger and larger amounts of government information are being labelled as confidential, as highly confidential, as secret, as top secret, as not for public distribution, as an interdepartmental communication, as a special study, as an advisory report or whatever the label that is applied.
In effect, we are seeing an attempt to block a basic democratic process, that of the right to know. In recent days we have had debates in the House touching on this very issue, and we are clearly seeing that on this question the government is using its opinion regarding the production of a particular document or paper as the criterion for deciding whether so to produce the information.
I think we must establish very clearly that there are basic ground rules in respect of the tabling of documents. Instead of adopting the attitude that whenever the government feels it necessary, it may maintain that things are confidential, we should reverse this trend and say that generally it is in the public interest to have this information unless it can be conclusively proved that documents if made public will create substantial harm in one form or another. Now it appears the burden of proof is the other way and members are drastically limited in this regard.
We know that at the end of a session, even at the end of a very brief one such as this, there remains a long list of motions which hon. members have brought forward for the production of papers. A few are adopted, fewer still are voted on, and most are completely ignored. I do not think this is good enough. I do not think a system of government as complex as the one we have evolved in this country can work effectively if information is increasingly denied the people and their representatives.
If ever there was proof of lack of policy and clear procedure for the House to deal with the production of papers, it was pointed out in yesterday afternoon's performance in this House. We would not need constantly to go through a repetition of the kind of thing the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and myself have done in respect of these specific papers on CIDA in Viet Nam if we had clear procedure and if there were a clear delineation as to what should be made public and under what conditions. At the present time this business is increasingly frustrating; it is frustrating to the point of delaying the work of government and denying public participation.
I think it is most difficult for any government spokesman to prove that the public does not have the right to know what has been our performance, policy and activity in respect of aid programs in such a sensitive situation as that in Viet Nam. I for one would be most interested to know why, particularly after a long passage of time, it is generally thought that reports submitted should not be made available. I should like to know why these reports cannot now be in the public domain. I think the burden of proving the necessity of maintaining them as confidential documents should be with the government. I will be very interested to hear what the government has to say in this instance.

Mr. Speaker, there are two aspects of this debate on the motion for the production of papers moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). One is the policy of the Canadian government in respect of the war in Viet Nam. Every debate on a motion for the production of papers brings with it a substantial discussion on the material that is said to be contained or may be contained in those papers. Then there is the question-this was raised in the last few minutes of the remarks of the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald)-of the confidentiality of documents exchanged between public servants and ministers of the Crown. Those are the two aspects of this debate.
With regard to the first aspect, the policy of the Canadian government on the war in Viet Nam, we on this side of the House do not accept the allegations of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and the hon. member for Egmont. During these remarks I shall not enter into the question of what is Canadian policy in respect of the war in Viet Nam or what it should or should not have been. I shall not engage in a refutation of the remarks of those who preceded me. That matter might better be discussed in a debate on external affairs which gives ample scope to discuss the substance of the question. I want to address myself particularly to the concluding remarks of the hon. member for Egmont when he spoke of confidential papers and what the government ought to do about them.
This motion provides a good case for examination. First of all, who is Dr. Vennema? That has been very ably dealt with by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. If I might just refresh the minds of hon. members for a moment, he was project director of the Canadian tuberculosis centre in Quang Ngai from 1965 to 1967. He was appointed director of Canadian medical services in Viet Nam shortly before his departure. Following the 1968 Tet offensive, he returned to Viet Nam briefly to report on the status of Canadian medical aid projects.
During his assignments in Viet Nam, Dr. Vennema prepared several reports for the government, including two following his February 12 to March 28, 1968, visit. He recommended, among other things, the withdrawal of all Canadian medical personnel from Viet Nam. He had some very vivid things to say about his experiences in Viet Nam. He is a person of great sincerity whose work and ability as a medical man won for him the medal of the Order of Canada. He is a man of unquestioned integrity and reputation. Having heard him speak on television following his assignment, I think he can only be regarded as a good Canadian with a message in which he sincerely believed and wanted to convey to the Canadian people.
The questions with which we must deal in the case of the papers of Dr. Vennema are: What was his relationship with the government, and what was his relationship in respect of the reports he submitted? There was a relationship of confidentiality. Whatever may have been said by Dr. Vennema subsequently in making his case, which he had a perfect right to do, he was at that time bound by confidentiality in his reports. I think he respected that fact in the reports he made to the Canadian government.
June 29, 1972

All experts such as Dr. Vennema who perform a particular service under contract-to CIDA in this case- submit reports on their projects as a matter of routine. These reports are part of the requirement of service and are all submitted on the understanding that they will be treated as confidential and privileged documents, because frequently they contain information and personal opinions about individuals as well as views about the projects in which they are involved.
These reports are of considerable importance in improving CIDA's assistance programs to developing countries and, in fact, in improving the ability of the government of Canada to assist in a particular situation. Public distribution by the government of such reports could be interpreted by the experts working for CIDA as a breach of confidence. Moreover, if it became the practice to make such reports public it would inhibit officials of CIDA or any other officials from expressing their views.
We must remember that confidentiality is part of the daily life of employers and employees working together in a particular situation. Confidentiality enters into our discussions in this House as the business of the House moves forward: there is confidentiality in respect of meetings of House leaders, confidentiality in conversations between whips, between members and ministers and between members on both sides of the House about the business we put forward.
If what was said by them were to be made into a press release, then what was said between employer and employee and what we said in this House to each other when discussing business in confidence, would be only what we were prepared to see printed for publication. So, if we were to move, as suggested by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), to a position where a report from a public servant could be made public unless, as he put it, it were conclusively proven that it would be harmful to the public interest, then we could be assured that the reports the government receives from its public servants in departments everywhere and abroad would contain only those matters which they were prepared to see published. In this event, the minister and the executives in the public service would know no more about what was going on than what they read in the papers. If confidentiality does not and cannot exist in documents of this kind, there would be no sense whatever in asking for a report from a man of Dr. Vennema's stature and undoubted integrity for he certainly would not report in all honesty what he felt if he believed his opinions were to be made public.
If we ask a man his opinion in confidence the answer will be different from one given for publication. This is something we all know.
Dr. Vennema wants it published.

The government of Canada has a position to maintain in respect of its public servants. If it took the position that it would, from time to time, pluck a confidential report out of the basket and make it public material, as is being suggested now by the hon. member,
Vennema Report on Viet Nam War
then all I can say is that public servants will report to their employers precisely the kind of material that the hon. gentleman and I see every day of our lives and shove into the wastepaper basket. That kind of material is cranked out by the public service day after day. We know a great deal about it. The scrap paper people become wealthy just carting away the press releases which contain that kind of information in the House of Commons.
This is not that type.

I know the kind of information to which the hon. gentleman is referring. He is referring to a confidential report made to the government of Canada, and made in confidence so that the government could make a judgment. I think we must respect our public servants and be prepared to deal with them in confidence. Although this is most unlikely, I say to the hon. member that if the day should ever come when he occupies a seat on this side of the House or a seat on the cabinet bench, I doubt very much that he would tell his senior officials that they should not tell him anything they do not want published because they would be likely to find themselves in a most embarrassing position since confidentiality between him and them had gone out the window. That is not really what the hon. member would do if he found himself in that position. Dr. Vennema knew that would not happen when he sent that report to the government of Canada advising the government about conditions.
Why does he say he wants it made public now?

I think that is a matter the hon. gentleman and others should take up with Dr. Vennema.
In closing, I simply want to make the point clear once more that there is no question about the confidential relationship which must exist between senior officials of the government of Canada and ministers in respect of reports. If that relationship cannot exist, they certainly cannot work together. That is the way it has been when other governments have been in power. That is the way it was when the Conservative government, the party of the hon. member for Egmont, was in power. That is how it would be if, as I say, it should ever fall to the NDP to form a government in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have prepared a speech which I should like to have enough time to deliver this afternoon. The hon. member made his own speech; therefore, I wish he gave me the same opportunity, after which he might ask his questions.
Dr. Vennema is recognized as a highly competent specialist who carried out the particular work entrusted to him in Vietnam most ably and successfully, on account of his medical knowledge and the human character he gave to his work there, in the circumstances known to all of us which prevailed in that area of the world then and unfortunately are still prevailing now. The high professional ability of Dr. Vennema is beyond any doubt. Besides, Canada has recognized his achievements.
Dr. Vennema is a Canadian who in the early 60s first worked in Vietnam, as stated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, under an American medical program designed to alleviate the plight of the civil population constantly pressed by the war actions that were and still are breaking up on that territory.
At the request of the Vietnamese government, Canada agreed to contribute to the construction, the equipment and the operation of a anti-tuberculosis centre. In accordance with that agreement, our country, under its foreign aid program administered by the Canadian International Development Agency, built a modest two-storey building. This country provided the necessary equipment and medical supplies, as well as a team of experts for ensuring the effective operation of that centre. On the other hand, the Vietnamese people provided the lot and shared the operating costs. The Canadian medical team included the project director, who was Dr. Vennema from 1965 to 1967, nurses, technicians and administrative personnel, whose tasks included management of the training given to the Vietnamese people who were eventually to take over the

administration of that centre and who in fact did so in 1972.
The centre which, by the way, is located in the city of Quangngai in the province of the same name, was inaugurated officially at the end of 1967 at which time Dr. Vennema was appointed director of the project. However, as a result of the events we are all aware of and which accompanied the Tet offensive early in 1968, the centre was closed temporarily and the Canadian medical staff pulled out of Quangngai. At the end of his tenure, in 1968, Dr. Vennema was replaced by Dr. Michel Jutras, who remained director from December 3, 1967 until July 6, 1971.
Mr. Speaker, Canada spent $2,000,000 on that anti-tuberculosis clinic project. The project has proved very efficient in that province of Viet Nam owing to the generous contribution of the Canadian personnel, including Dr. Vennema and other Canadians just mentioned.
In fact, the responsibility for that project has been transferred to the Minister of Health of South Viet Nam on March 22, 1972, and all the Canadians who were affected completed their contract and left QuangNgai as expected.
During his stay in Viet Nam, Dr. Vennema has naturally prepared and presented several reports on behalf of the Canadian government including two in 1968, in order to evaluate the consequences of the Tet offensive. Among other things, these reports recommended, as said earlier, the withdrawal of all Canadian medical personnel from Vietnam as of 1968. Later on, Dr. Vennema made the newspapers' headlines by commenting the use of poison gas in Vietnam, the massacre of Vietnamese civilians and the presence of Canadians.
As for Mrs. Culhane, whose name was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, on her arrival in Vietnam she criticized the Canadian policy and presence in that country. Apparently, at least from the newspapers' reports on Mrs. Culhane and Dr. Vennema, their criticisms were rather of a political nature and were not in the least aimed at the high quality of the Canadian medical assistance to the Vietnamese civil population and how welcome was this assistance in Vietnam. The issue of Vietnam policy had nothing to do with the assignment of the Canadians who went there to establish hospitals. In fact, part of Dr. Vennema's report recommended the creation of several hospitals and this recommendation was implemented by Canada; several hospitals have been set up throughout Vietnam.
Over the last two years, similar motions have been introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) doubtlessly following the failure of the "Voice of Women" in their efforts to obtain copies of those reports and correspondence and also following the repeated criticisms from Mrs. Culhane. The department refused to release the reports prepared by the advisers of the Canadian International Development Agency because they are considered as classified and, as I said earlier, I think that in the public interest those documents should be recognized as such.

Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment hour I had been speaking about the difficulties that would be created under this bill because of the bureaucracy that will be necessary to monitor family income as a result of the adoption of this plan. I had an opportunity to reread the remarks I made on March 28 when this bill was before the House for second reading. At that time I referred to the administrative nightmare that would be created. I have not changed my mind one iota in the interval. As a matter of fact, I think the committee hearings have confirmed the fact that the administration of the bill will create a great deal of difficulty.
Family Income Security Plan
Seemingly the public has been lulled into a false sense of security as a result of the lengthy interval between second reading and now, when the government insists on coming back with the bill in the dying hours of this session of Parliament in an effort to get it accepted. The bill is political window dressing, Mr. Speaker. I am not quarrelling personally with the minister on this score. I blame the whole administration for it. I have said the same thing with regard to Bill C-201, the so-called takeovers bill. I predict that we will see some more bits and pieces of legislation tossed out during the course of the summer in an attempt to make sweeter to the Canadian public what up to now has been a very unpalatable situation in the anticipation of the possibility of a fall election. Indeed, the context of an election must be considered in connection with all these matters.
In a constituency of the kind I represent, this type of bill is resented. In view of all the protestations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with regard to the social egalitarianism that he talks about, and his plan for an attempted redistribution of income, obviously he does not believe in the doers in this country. He believes in the non-doers. He neglects the fact that what makes this country go forward, what pays my salary, pays the minister's salary, pays the member's salary, and pays for all of the so-called income adjustments, is that section of the people who are the doers.
The hon. member speaks about a built-in welfare society. Those are the non-doers. We are building more and more of them into our society. I fully agree with the change; it has been the philosophy of my party for a number of years. This bill is part of a re-examination of our whole welfare structure in order to put the emphasis where it is needed. We should put our funds, and the good Lord knows they are limited even though my friends to the left think they are unlimited, where they will do the most good. If a man needs two blankets, it is no answer to give him and another each half a blanket. All too often this is what we do. I look at the whole government plan. Within the family allowance plan, I will recognize the principle of universality to the extent that the allowance be paid for each child but when we come to the income tax that should be based on ability to pay. We may disagree with some of the details, but we agree that the criteria for taxation should be the ability to pay.
In the province of Ontario, the ability to pay is the basis of the program for grants to individuals with lower incomes. In order to recover this amount, those with the ability pay a higher proportion of sales tax, customs duties and so forth. We should be heading in this direction. The formula in this bill is a step out of pace with the general formula that we place our funds where they will do the most good. If the amounts are to be $15 and $20,1 am quite prepared to accept that. However, I do not accept the minister's statement that those amounts shall be the net cost to government. By making the family allowance universal, those at the higher income level will pay an increased proportion of that allowance back to the government on the basis of their marginal rates. After all, we are doing that with unemployment insurance and the retraining allowance. We are making them repayable to government at the marginal rate of the tax payer, so why not here?
Some of my friends have a high income of $30,000 or $35,000 a year net. How do they do that? They work 16 hours a day, sometimes seven days a week. They have eight or nine children and they work like beavers. Even though these people pay a good deal of income tax, they would still keep 50 per cent of their family allowance. They do not feel penalized because, even though they have a large family, they work hard for their family. As such they must not be penalized. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us tonight the 1972 edition of the family allowances or, as indicated in this bill, of the benefits in respect of children.
Clause 1 of the bill accurately states the range of this legislation regarding family income security plan. Clause 2 deals with definitions and we can sum it up as follows: this clause is important since it must be constantly referred to when considering the bill. For example "the base calendar year" means the year for which the family income is computed and on the basis of which benefits claimed are determined.
Moreover, subclause 2(2) contains a definition of a person's income for a calendar year, which is his income computed for income tax purposes minus death benefits paid under a pension plan.
It should be noted that, in accordance with the legislation, the family income to be considered for the family income security plan is computed by adding the income of both the father and the mother.
Clause 3 provides that benefits will be paid out of the Consolidated Fund in respect of each child less than 18 years of age who is maintained by a person resident in Canada. Should a province pay any benefits in respect of children between the ages of 16 and 18, as is the case with Quebec, then no benefits are payable to these persons by the federal government if the latter provides tax abatements in this regard to the province.
How will the amount of benefit be determined? This is dealt with in clause 6 of the bill which is unquestionably the most important and most complex of them all.
First of all, monthly benefits of $15 for children less than 12 years old are provided. There are also monthly benefits of $20 for children aged 12 or more but under 18.
As clause 6(l)(a), (b) and (c) indicate, there is a ceiling on the income of families. And when the family income is equal to or over that ceiling, the allowances decrease insofar as children are concerned and become nil according to the income or the number of children.
Now we come to the most interesting part of the scheme: the computation formula. In the case of an only child, the amount of the allowance proposed by the minister-$15 or $20-will be reduced by 33 cents for every $100 over the family income of $4,500.

When there is more than one child, in order to understand the computation, the basic income eligible must be added, namely $4,500 plus $500 per child in excess of one to obtain the basis of the computation. Then one has to proceed as I outlined above in the case of an only child.
Here is an example, Mr. Speaker, to show what boat we are getting in. Let us suppose the case of an only child. The family income is $6,000; by subtracting the allowed income of $4,500, one gets $1,500. Now as the rate decreases by 33 cents for each $100, there would be a decrease of $4.95. The allowance for a child under 12 would therefore be $10.05
In the case of children from 12 to 18, the $20 allowance would be reduced to $15.05.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) says the calculation is easy since I managed to figure it out. I recognize that I did, but I owe my thanks to the research service.
But, Mr. Speaker, the citizen s of our riding will never be able to manage that complicated calculation.
If a family with two children has an income of $6,000, the basic income will be $4,500 plus $500, that is $5,000. The hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) should listen: he would learn something! In that case, the allowance would be reduced by $3.30, that is 10 times 33. The allowance for a child under 12 would therefore be $15 less $3.30, that is $11.70, and for the child between 12 and 18, of $20. less $3.30, that is $16.70.
Such is the calculated munificence of the government! Instead of paying a universal benefit for all children, the government is basing it on income.
Let us consider the case of a family with four children, Mr. Speaker. Since up to now some members have been unable to understand I will quote them more figures. They should listen and wait afterwards to make jokes.
In the case of a family with four children, since the allowable income is $6,000-that is $4,500 plus 3 times $500 or $1,500-the basic benefits will be $15 for each child under 12 and $20 for each child from 12 to 18 years of age.
If a family has 5, 6, 8 or 10 children, the benefits will be the same because they will have reached the maximum amount.
For an income of $8,000-Mr. Speaker, I always expect to be called back to order because my speech does not deal with family allowances but with mathematics-the following computation is made: $8,000 less $4,500, that is $3,500. The decreasing rate is 33 cents for each full $100, so the reduction will be 25 times 33 cents or $11.55 The benefit for a child under 12 will be $15 less $11.55, that is $3.45.
It may have cost $50, $100 or $200 for public servants to make the calculations, to print the forms, to mail and return them because of mistakes, etc., in order, finally, to pay only $3.45.

For a child between 12 and 18, the allowance will be $20 minus $11.55, or $8.45. For two children, and a family income of $8,000, the maximum income allowed is $4,500. If $500 is added it makes $5,000. So, $8,000 minus $5,000 makes $3,000. Let us multiply each $100 by 33 cents and we get $9.90. The allowance will be $15 minus $9.90, or $5.10, a very generous allowance from this government as a reward to a couple for having earned $8,000 in one year. For children 12 to 18, the allowance will be $20 minus $9.90, or $10.10. That is the reward that this couple is getting for having worked.
For a family of 4 children with an $8,000 income, if you make the famous calculation, $4,500 plus $500 multiplied by 3, or $6,000, then substracted from $8,000, you get $2,000. Twenty times 33 cents make $6.60. So, for a child under 12, the allowance will be $15 minus $6.60 or $8.40. We go backwards instead of forward. For children 12 to 18, if $6.60 is substracted from $20, the benefit amounts to $13.40.
I have in mind another case, Mr. Speaker. This one is a little more serious. I am thinking about the minister's "jokes". Here is a real and not so funny case. The husband's income is $6,000 and he is entitled to benefits. Of course often on investigation he gets them. But he cannot make ends meet. Once food, housing, clothing and care are paid for with $6,000 and three children, it is impossible to manage financially. And Mr. Speaker, there are many Canadian families with a $6,000 income. I will call to mind the Croll report on poverty. This will give you a good idea of the situation. A couple with three children cannot live.
So the husband and wife talk things over. They try hard to find a solution and the wife says: there's no choice; I must find a job. This happens often also. The wife decides therefore to go to work if she can find a job of course. Let us say that she is paid $4,000. This is quite reasonable. My colleagues agree on $4,000. That means they have just lost their family allowances. With $6,000, that couple cannot make ends meet. They decide to make sacrifices, to divide the family in some way, making immense sacrifices to make ends meet and bring up their three children, and because the wife is working, because she has earned an income, she will be rewarded by the loss of family allowances.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the system the minister wants to force on us tonight. It is a negative system, whereby the more you try to help yourself, the harder you try to get along and improve your own lot, the less assistance and the more kicks in the pants you get from the government.
However, the government does not forget to give fantastic fiscal advantages to both Canadian and foreign corporations. And they call that a "just society." To my way of thinking, family allowances, or benefits paid regarding children, mean financial assistance to the family, for the maintenance of children. I consider them as a calculated handout. They should, instead, be a spontaneous gift from the government, without selfish motives, without complications, without civil servants and without confounded bureaucracy. Let them make a spontaneous gift to children and families, instead of discouraging them.
In other words, Bill C-170 proposes to increase benefits to $15 and $20 and administration costs will be as high as the benefits paid.

Mr. Speaker, a family whose head earns $10,000, $11,000 or $12,000 a year, and which has 5, 6 or 7 children will not get a penny in family allowances.
A family whose income is $12,000 and which has 6 or 7 children will find itself penalized because it has worked too hard or has too many children.
I would like to end my remarks here and say that I object to this bill. I strongly oppose the principle of selectivity. In my view, it is not up to the government to determine who has a right to live in Canada; the government must ensure that everybody has the right to live in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, selectivity is therefore a monstruous and unthinkable concept; the government has no right to pester people like that, and its first moral obligation is to support efforts made by Canadians.
It is not only in that field that we are negative, Mr. Speaker.
As I was saying a while ago, if the head of a family who earns $6,000 cannot make both ends meet his wife will look for a job. Afterwards this couple will receive $10,000 and, as a reward, will lose their family allowances.
Mr. Speaker, at least two answers can be handed me in this regard: the wife should not go to work and all the government has to do is to set up the income security plan. It will have to do it because either this couple cannot make both ends meet, or they earn a sufficient amount of money to do without allowances.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if this second proposal is justified, the hon. minister should not lower the eligibility age but rather the amount of eligible income. One can easily see that this is a stupid reasoning. Therefore the principle of selectivity based on the combined income of husband and wife is meaningless.
There is another thing that one must keep in mind: that is, a child of a family whose income amounts to $4,000 should be entitled to the same rights as the child in a family whose income amounts to $10,000. The child in a family whose income amounts to $10,000 must enjoy, if all Canadians are equal, the same rights as the other one, whose family is poorer. The government may say that it means a waste of money. Its tax policy-which is
June 29, 1972

described in 190 pages-will easily compensate this by taxing the people. There is no problem here. Our tax experts can find enough money to pay for these benefits. Let us recognize at least this basic right to every child in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the minister should not bring in a negative bill which discourages the individual, but rather a positive one. The bill now before us is ridiculous! To be entitled to allowances, we must revamp our whole welfare system, in order to arrive at a meaningful and positive overall policy.
As to the welfare allowances, Mr. Speaker, the less a man works, the less he helps himself; the more he abides by officialdom, the more he bows before officials to get his public assistance, the more he gets. The more he tries to help himself, the more he tries to work, to find a job or to perform a small job of some sort to add to his income, the lower the welfare allowances. Governments will then say that people are lazy. And the same governments have established those negative programs which discourage the individual. The law says: the less you help yourself, the more money you get.
As to unemployment insurance, the first condition to get benefits is not to work. That is very positive. That is ridiculous. The second condition is to be available for work. According to the law, what does the expression to be available for work mean? It means a man remains at home, does not limit his availability to one city and is ready to accept any job anywhere in Canada. In any event, the person knows no one will call and waits for the unemployment insurance cheques. These will even be paid for up to 51 weeks.
Mr. Speaker, on examining the FISP legislation, one sees it is well drawn up. The same goes for the bill on family allowances. Close examination of the unemployment insurance act also under which up to $90 or $92 a week are paid the unemployed, reveals that it too is well drawn up. But if we study them together within the social security system in Canada we realize that the basic philosophy of those various bills which are intended to improve the lot of Canadians is negative, so that more and more Canadians depend on the various governments to live and survive, when the opposite should be true.
Mr. Speaker, an ever increasing number of Canadians are living off a decreasing working minority and, according to the new bill passed by the House, from now on the middle class will pay for others and through the nose.
In this regard, socialists say: Take some away from the rich, and give it to the poor. That is exactly what the minister does with this bill. He says: Take some away from the rich-$10,000, and God knows that is not much in Canada in view of the constant increase in the cost of living-and give it to the poor. This is a socialistic bill, Mr. Speaker.
The government will then tell us: Let us establish a just society where each citizen can live freely, enjoy security, and grow to full maturity in his own country. It is perfectly ridiculous and inconsistent.
Mr. Speaker, I urgently request social measures to guarantee income security to each Canadian citizen without any red tape or investigation so that he will automatically receive his benefits as his share of the national production
Business of the House
which reaches $100 billion a year. A bare minimum should be provided for each Canadian citizen and we should refrain from harassing him. I have enough confidence in my fellow citizens to know that they will make way and not live off the fat of the land.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding I will point out that this bill brings up the entire philosophy of the government on social security legislation. I say to the minister that I will vote against his bill because it is one step closer to socialism, a measure which will annoy people and create huge problems with forms, paper work and red tape. What will the bill provide in the long run for the people?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought last night that perhaps this bill might pass and there would be no further debate on it. However, I would like at this time to bring to the attention of the House some of the difficult problems that agriculture faces. The fact that the government has brought forward this bill is an admission on their part that there are serious difficulties in agriculture and that provisions must be brought in to assist people who engage in the production of agricultural products throughout the country.
On second reading we moved an amendment which was turned down by the government. It was brought forward in an attempt to provide incentives for young farmers who become involved in agriculture, to initiate better programs to enable young people to get started, and to assist those people whom the government is trying to remove from the farms. We believe that incentives should be given to young people to stay on the farm.
This bill provides a little more money. The amount of $56 million has been increased to $66 million in the financial resources of the Farm Credit Corporation. I believe this was done in recognition of the fact that more money is needed to help young people stay on the farm and to assist those engaged in farming to carry on. The bill also provides that loans will be granted to facilitate efficient operation of a farm. Under the present act, loans are available only if the money is necessary for efficient operation. I must admit that this is a move in the right direction-away from negative, last resort aid, to more positive help. This seems to be action taken before last-ditch efforts become necessary- Any move in that direction will, I am sure, be a good thing for the agricultural industry.
Also, under this bill loans will become available to persons under 21 years of age. Previously they were not able to obtain loans, but this legislation brings the age requirement down to 18. In addition, farm improvement loans which are available through the banks can now be obtained without a prior commitment from the Farm Credit Corporation. This seems to be reasonable and will provide money to those engaged in agriculture. It will cut down the red tape which so frequently exists in these matters.
Then in this bill the appraised value of land will include the productive value of a second non-farming enterprise that might be carried on by the same individual. I suggest
Farm Credit Act
that this provision may not be all bad: it will be possible to get an increased loan on a smaller parcel of land. The amendments in this bill are good but in our estimation they are not good enough. We would have liked the bill to include a provision for partial non-repayment of loans when young farmers meet certain performance standards. Before anyone in the NDP jumps up and says young farmers would have to be perfect before qualifying, I would point out that "performance standards" simply means meeting the payments they agreed to meet when they obtained loans.
We also would have liked a provision in the bill that interest payments in the initial period of a loan could be delayed, so that a new enterprise could show some results in a financial way before a farmer had to repay large commitments. However, the government majority voted against us on that suggestion.
Some government members suggested that we would not support this bill. This is not true, Mr. Speaker. They seem to enjoy preaching throughout the country that we oppose for the sake of opposing rather than for the sake of being constructive. This is not true. The measures proposed in this legislation are not that bad, but we say they could be a lot better; and at second reading, committee stage, report stage, and now on third reading, we have endeavoured to improve the legislation. In the House of Commons our aim is to improve legislation. If government members complain that they have trouble getting legislation through the House, it is because government legislation has often been hastily brought forward, ill conceived, and has not served a purpose satisfactory to the people of the country.
I am disappointed that the government stood fast in upholding clause 1 of the bill, giving them all kinds of power, without offering any real explanation of how that power would be used. We voted on that matter last night. I am happy to say that I registered my vote against it.
There are all kinds of precedents for providing incentives to new borrowers. CMHC has provision for partial non-repayment of loans. During the last four years incentives have been provided to various businesses to start operations all across the country. The Financial Administration Act gives the government power to forgive a tax, penalty or debt, in particular cases. If housing and business can receive these incentives, why cannot agriculture have the same privilege? It is often said that what is good for business is good for the country. This was preached by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his last budget. I suggest that what is good for the farmer is also good for the country.
The major industry in the constituency of Huron is agriculture. As agriculture goes, so goes the economy of Huron county. So long as I have the privilege of being a member of the House of Commons, agriculture and its betterment will be one of my first priorities. It is disappointing that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) did not see fit to accept some of the amendments put forward by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). Had he done so, this would be a much better bill.

June 29, 1972
Farm Credit Act
The government seems to think that those engaged in agriculture are to be used only to produce cheap food, so that in turn industry may have a chance to export industrial products to other countries. This is not acceptable. If farmers received a profitable return for their products, it would have an expansionary effect all across the country. If the primary producers had dollars in their pockets, they would become purchasing consumers of the industrial products which provide jobs.
We also urged the provision of open-ended loans, that loans could be increased without going through all the red tape involved in obtaining the original loan. One report shows that of the $115.2 million in loans approved during 1970-71, $36.4 million went to repay existing loans. We do not disagree with the provision of additional money for loans to single family farm operations, up to the amount of $100,000; but if the government had listened to our suggestions this would be a better bill. We have offered good suggestions but the government has not listened to us.
We have offered suggestions of the type that would make the Liberal party popular, but they seem to feel that they know all, control all, can do all and are the only people who ought to govern. I suggest they had better start listening, for before long they will discover that what they think is not true.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my remarks on the third reading debate I wish to make three points briefly. First, we in my party feel that the small farms section of the bill is somewhat vague and we are under the impression that the government itself is not too clear as to what it wants in this regard. Second-and I am still talking about the first point-it appears there is some overlapping of provincial and federal jurisdiction. This applies especially to Saskatchewan. Apparently two acts, one federal and the other provincial, are concerned in the administration of similar types of programs. I have suggested this before but wish to repeat my suggestion now for the benefit of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). If two, similar programs are to be run by two levels of government, then those governments should join hands and turn them into a single program.

speechtext:
In any event, I am sure the minister can speak for himself; he is pretty eloquent. I suggest to the minister that he should not rush in and implement these small farm provisions before he has worked out the

details of the program with the provinces concerned, because we do not want duplication in this area. I am concerned about this and I hope he is.
Second, I suggest that the Farm Credit Corporation should look carefully at how much money it will lend against land of certain value. I am concerned about land values. Although I support that the corporation has done in the past with regard to farm credit loans, I feel that some actions of the Farm Credit Corporation tended to force up land prices. People have bid more per acre and values have increased. This has left some farmers in an awkward position. They have found it hard to repay loans. I want to emphasize this point.
Officials of the Farm Credit Corporation, along with farmers and governments, were getting very excited over the large wheat sales made to Russia and to China. This excitement was evident in my province. Consequently, some farmers when they bought land paid prices which were unrealistic. The Farm Credit Corporation helped them to pay these prices. I draw to the attention of the minister and Farm Credit Corporation officials that these farmers are not very happy. Some of them are behing the 8-ball, so to speak, and cannot meet their interest payments. This is a regrettable situation. That is not how we ought to use funds provided or subsidized by the government. I do not think anyone intended that to happen, but happen it did as a result of an oversight or error. I feel the Farm Credit Corporation was in error in this regard.
Third, I should like to emphasize again that not all agricultural problems are to be solved by lending money. It is sometimes thought that if farms were bigger they would become more efficient, that big farmers can produce barley for 64 cents a bushel and oats for 40-odd cents a bushel. I suggest that this is not necessarily so because factors other than borrowing are involved in farm economics. In other words, you cannot, in all circumstances borrow your way out of trouble.
Of course, those who need to borrow money will be helped by this legislation and that is its intent. However, let us not be carried away by the idea that we can borrow our way out of trouble. Price is important too. The minister from Saskatoon-Humboldt seems to think that an increased volume of sales will solve our problems. Volume is important, I agree, but price is also important. Mr. Speaker, those are the three points I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of this bill, I should like to say a couple of words about it.
Having had the advantage of sitting on the Committee on Agriculture for four years, I should like to say that this bill is of a very great significance and has definitely a very great value. In fact, this bill completes remarkably well the farm legislation that this government has passed during the past four years.
I know that in my riding, they have succeeded, through favorable farm measures, in stabilizing the dairy industry so that producers may derive a satisfactory income from it.
June 29, 1972

I think also of Bill C-176 which, thanks to the co-operation of the officials of the agencies concerned and of the provinces, will also bring forth quite interesting improvements.
And we sire now considering Bill C-5 which will enable some agencies to take out loans in order to consolidate incurred debts following certain difficulties with some farm products. On the other hand, this legislation will enable agencies to make investment permitting them to operate a more profitable business.
It is clear, as the previous speaker said, that loans will not solve problems but I think that even so they are important for those who are thinking in terms of growth because we are now aware that expansion is absolutely necessary to enable the producer to get an adequate income and meet competition.
I would like to say a word about the repurchasing program regarding small farms. The minister's objective is fine but I am a little concerned about the bill. Discussions with the provinces, more precisely possible agreements with them regarding the program dealing with the management or repurchasing of small farms do not seem to have been completed. The minister has clearly indicated to the committee and in the House that he did intend to apply that program. How can this program be 100 per cent efficient if one, two, three or four provinces refuse to co-operate with the federal government? I think it is time to say it and I invite the minister to do his utmost to give evidence that this program is efficient and will benefit the provinces.
I should also like to invite the minister to show very great understanding about the provinces' priorities. It is something that we should respect. We know very well that on account of different conditions and mentalities, some provincial priorities are very different from those of the federal government.
I should not like to prolong my comments unduly, nor to insinuate that this problem can be settled without agreement. Quite the opposite, I have confidence in the understanding and ability of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and in view of his respect for the provinces I am sure he will manage to hold prior consultations with them and demonstrate that it is in the common interest to seek solutions resulting in suitable agreements while respecting provincial priorities, which the federal government might consider as difficult to accept. However, whatever the province involved the producers should not lose the great benefits which Bill C-5 nevertheless does provide.
Mr. Speaker, I have made these few comments merely as an appeal to the minister's consideration of the importance of respecting provincial priorities, without however neglecting the benefits of this legislation for any producer wishing to avail himself thereof.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the time my comments will be brief. I want to make a couple of points before the bill is read the third time. My principal point is this: if the minister feels this bill will solve many of the problems of prairie farmers and others, he is mistaken. Basically, this bill does two things, one of which I am very concerned about. First, it
Farm Credit Act
gives additional power to the Farm Credit Corporation. That is in clause 1 of Bill C-5 which is before us, which provides:
The corporation has all the powers necessary to carry out such duties or functions as may be assigned to it by the governor in council in relation to the administration of any agricultural program or as are assigned to it pursuant to any other act of the Parliament of Canada.
Under that clause we know that the minister's intention is to bring in through the back door the small farms development plan. I do not judge this to be democratic, I do not think it is what most people think of as parliamentary democracy about which members opposite talk so much. Many farm people in western Canada are very concerned about that program and the report of the task force on agriculture. I do not want to see this clause in the bill become the opening for the small farms development plan and many recommendations of the task force, especially without their being debated in this House. I say this very seriously because I know that most farmers are concerned.
I wish to read a short quotation from the statement made by the National Farmers Union when in Ottawa:
The National Farmers Union has called for rejection of a government bill to amend the Farm Credit Act because it "is designed to move farmers off the land and move land out of agricultural production."
This is a fear of the farmers' union. In my opinion, and in the opinion of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave), our party's spokesman on agriculture, the minister has not given adequate answers to questions such as those raised by the National Farmers Union and others concerned about agriculture and rural life in this country. I think he should provide us with those answers. He should not use this bill as an excuse to bring in the small farms development plan which has many ramifications for the rural life style, farmers and those living in small towns and villages on the Prairies. Our small farms are being eliminated quickly enough. According to Statistics Canada, between 1966 and 1971 the number of farms in this country decreased by 15 per cent. The minister should seriously consider this. I believe that the members of this House who represent urban Canada take this fact very seriously.
Many members from urban Canada have a good understanding of farming and rural life, but many people have the mistaken conception that the farmer is not efficient. He is very efficient. Figures show that in the past 10 to 20 years, the farmer's efficiency has gone up at twice the rate of the non-agricultural sector. The farmer is very productive; he knows how to manage his affairs and business.
The problem is that in the past 20 years the farmer's income has increased by only 20 per cent while his costs have doubled. No wonder the farmer is being forced off the land. The price he receives for commodities such as wheat and eggs has gone down between 1950 and 1970 despite the rise in the cost of production. I could elaborate, but that in a nutshell is the problem facing the farmer. That is why I am very concerned about clause 1.
If the small farms development plan is to be introduced, it should be as a separate bill so that we, the people's

June 29, 1972
Representation Commissioner Act representatives who are concerned can debate the bill, move amendments and offer suggestions. If implemented, this move can change the life of many people in rural Canada and, indeed, in many of the urban centres in this country.
My second point is that this bill will raise the ceiling of borrowing from a maximum of $48,000 to a maximum of $100,000. This may be necessary in many cases, but the area of Saskatchewan that I represent is primarily comprised of small and middle-sized farms. Although a clause like this probably will not do any harm, it will not do much good. I recommend that the minister seriously consider subsidizing interest rates for small farmers. For example, on loans up to $30,000 there should be an interest rate of either 3 per cent, 3} per cent or a maximum of 4 per cent. This would really help to keep the average guy on the farm, and would preserve rural Canada.
These are the points about which I am concerned. I am not satisfied with clause 1.1 urge the minister to reconsider some of the ideas and suggestions put forward in this debate, as well as the suggestions of farm organizations, the National Farmers Union, the Federation of Agriculture, wheat pools and others.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE AN INCREASE IN SALARY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like an explanation from the government as to why this bill is being introduced. We are aware that there have been changes in other government departments and that probably this department has not kept pace because it is under a specific act. It is a rather unique kind of job that operates on a ten-year basis. If we pass this bill we shall, in effect, be providing one man with $400,000 for doing a job which has to be carried out only when a census is taken and the electoral boundaries are redefined.

It seems to me that rather than make the change in the bill as proposed, we should relate the salary of this office to the salaries of deputy ministers, for example, in accordance with whatever criteria are used in those cases. The method used for making this change is similar to that used when we are changing our own salaries. In either case it does not meet with my approval. It is true this gentleman is in a unique position. No one is inclined to raise any particular objection to his salary or he might find his constituency going to Siberia and back.
I am not prepared to move an amendment, but it seems that we are making a long-term salary adjustment covering a ten-year period. If conditions continue in the future as they have in the past, the salary we are talking about today may end up being no more suitable than it was previously. We should consider arriving at an appropriate formula to cover the salaries of people such as Members of Parliament, the Auditor General, the Representation Commissioner and others in that category so that it will not be necessary to pick out individuals and make salary adjustments for them on a periodic basis. Their salaries would then be adjusted in the same way as those of senior officials in government departments.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE AN INCREASE IN SALARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed that this should be the only change being made in the legislation. There is some ground for advocating a wider review of the operations of this act. While I recognize that the motives for which the original act was introduced, the desire to take the redistribution of constituency boundaries out of the arena of politics, I believe it should be admitted that there are some shortcomings in the system.
Two changes are needed if we are to arrive at a basis. First, provision should be made to take into account representations from the public before the original set of boundaries is drawn by the provincial commissions. Once those boundaries are drawn, they tend to be fixed and it is difficult to secure meaningful changes. The second point is this and I present it as a personal view: I still feel that final responsibility for the approval of electoral boundaries must rest with the legislators of this country. They are the people who should take the final responsibility for any changes which are made.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the passage of this bill but I should like to point out that in this particular year the Representation Commissioner will be engaged in the very heavy task of participating in the work of the ten provincial commissions. Shortly-as a matter of fact tomorrow, or within a few days-the governor in council will be making public, on the recommendation of His Honour the Speaker, the names of the ten provincial commissioners. The Representation Commissioner is, of course, a member of each of the provincial commissions: thus, he will be carrying a heavy burden. It is for this reason that we are proposing that his salary should be equal to that of the Chief Electoral Officer or, as it is stated in the bill, equal to that of a judge of the Federal Court of Canada. It would be unfortunate if we were to lose the services of a commissioner who had rendered such valuable service to the country as an official of Parliament.
June 29, 1972

Having said this, I agree with the point made by the hon. member for Timiskaming about the need to review the role of Representation Commissioner. The commissioner himself has indicated in testimony before the standing committee that some changes will have to be made because the burden of work in the off years is not great enough to justify the maintenance of the full-time services of any particular person, especially the present commissioner.
It is clear to me that some changes will have to be made, but it did not seem wise to introduce changes just as we were on the threshold of a major redistribution and because of my feeling that members of the House would wish to make use of the services of the most experienced man in the field. Having said this, I would certainly undertake that after the present redistribution the standing committee will have an opportunity to give immediate consideration to what permanent arrangement ought to be made in connection with this particular function. It seems to me the matter ought to be considered along the line of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Timiskaming.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED INADEQUATE QUOTA FOR NEWFOUNDLAND IN PROVISION OF WORK UNDER STUDENT SUMMER EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 20 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson) a question regarding the summer student employment program which was part of the Opportunities for Youth program. The government had expounded the magnificence of this great program and announced that there would be 15,000 extra jobs created for students.
I realize that on the "late show" debate the answers we receive are dictated by the department, but before I receive an answer tonight from the parliamentary secretary I want to tell him that I do not agree with the answer he is going to give me. Out of these 15,000 student jobs this summer, 10,000 will be allocated under program No. 3, which relates to the regular student militia and reserve. This has been an ongoing program for many years although other new programs have been announced. This leaves only 5,000 student summer employment opportunities, which to my mind is not realistic.
In the province of Newfoundland, student unemployment is very high and the need for jobs there is greatest. Over-all, I agree with the student militia and ancillary programs; I think it is one of the good programs announced by the government. But it seems that the government does not give highest priority to areas of high unemployment.
Another thing that bothers me relates to program No. 4, which is citizenship and community assistance. Students in the militia are given jobs relating to community assistance, consisting of cleaning up projects and other tasks which employ them for the summer. In Newfoundland, 50 students have been allocated to this program so that in the capital city of St. John's, Newfoundland, a military tattoo can be held on Signal Hill.
This is another program that has been ongoing for many years. These people were taken out of the militia, which is under category 3, and shifted into category 4 under citizenship and community assistance. This means that the 50 personnel allocated to the one program were taken out of the military portion and put into another category which has nothing to do with the military tattoo. This leaves the province of Newfoundland with not one allocation under category 3. This surprises me because every other province has a good allocation and I wonder why the Atlantic region has again been left out.
I do not think the deadline arrives until July 10, so I would ask the parliamentary secretary to urge the minister to reconsider the situation. I have said on a number of occasions that this is one of the best programs the government has ever introduced. I commend the government for it. If it intends to put on a program, why does it tell the people of Canada it will involve a certain number when in reality in involves a much lower number?
In the community in which I live I have experienced 25 years of militia service and that service has allocated 50 people to this program. From information I have received, the allocation will now only be 30. If this is a good program for Canada, I do not think we should be told this is

what the government is doing when in fact there is no intention of carrying it out. This is a good program and it creates the opportunity of raising a bit of money in order that the students can continue their education.
It also creates the opportunity for building up our militia and reserve forces. I say this facetiously because the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) and his predecessors for 25 years have been telling me at meetings of the Canadian Infantry Association that great things are happening in the militia, that we have a great bunch of officers and that the militia will do a great service for the country. Contrary to that, what has been happening over the past 25 years has been a steady deterioration of the militia. Certainly that is true of the militia in Newfoundland.
If the present policies are continued, it will not be long before the reserve forces become ineffective and eventually deteriorate to nothing. I ask the parliamentary secretary to pass on my representations to the minister, so that he will tell the militia officers who have performed great service over the years what is going to happen to the militia and whether this program is to be continued. Let them know what is going on, rather than telling them something of a negligible nature.
