maintopic: INDUSTRY-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PREVENT CLOSURE OF PORT MOODY PLANT OF CASCADE-DELTA BENCO COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I being to the House tonight a very sad tale which unfortunately under this government has been replicated far too many times all over our country. My specific concern tonight is with approximately 150 employees of the Cascade-Delta Benco Company of Port Moody, in my riding, which plans to close its operation in the next three months and move its operation and manufacturing unit into the golden triangle of the Toronto area.
We in western Canada constantly decry the concentration of secondary and tertiary industry in central Canada, forcing the principal economic preoccupation in western Canada on primary resource and extraction industries. What we in western Canada are losing is an industry of tremendous growth and export potential at a time when western sensitivities are much aroused against the concentration of manufacturing in specifically one area of the country.
To understand completely the motivation behind the Cascade plant closure one must go back in history at least five years. Perhaps before we indulge in the flashback we should know that recently Cascade merged with Delta-Benco of Rexdale, Ontario, an 80 per cent British-owned firm which manufacturers a complementary line of cable television equipment to that of Cascade in my riding. But long before the merger it must be said that Cascade, which is a west coast firm managed by men who are pioneers in the cable TV industry, attempted apparently
June 29, 1972

without much success to secure federal government assistance in one form or another.
I am told that in spite of their access to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, lubricated by Members of Parliament from British Columbia, all the management of Cascade got was the brush-off by the department. With an export record of between $11 million and $2 million to the United States, and because of the quality of their product which is six months ahead of similar products anywhere else in the world, and unsurpassed, Cascade tried to interest the government in two basic ideas. Cascade asked for federal backing or guarantees on export sales of about 90 per cent in case the corporation in the foreign country declined to honour its indebtedness upon receiving the import from Cascade. This is neither a wild nor a particularly radical suggestion: it is done in many other countries interested in enhancing their export position.
Second, Cascade requested government backing in order to finance sales, both foreign and domestic, somewhat in the manner that large U.S. multicorporations in similar fields are able to do when a cable television distributing company wishes to use a certain manufacturer's product to wire a city or suburb. They need that kind of financing to advance the sale in this instance. But all Cascade got from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was stony silence. They never met the minister, so far as I know, and I understand it has been suggested that the Cascade principals did not receive a better reception mainly because Cascade was, in the opinion of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, under-financed in terms of equity capital and much too dependent on loan or debt capital.
With the decision to move the plant, all these details are really irrelevant when it comes to giving 150 jobs in my riding of Fraser Valley West. Some of the people who will be unemployed are undoubtedly subscribers to the same group of companies which owned Cascade originally before they merged with Delta.
What we must address ourselves to, I think, is how we might reverse this decision which was occasioned by a reported loss of something like $200,000 per year on Cascade's operations, regardless of the fact that CRTC foreign-ownership limitations of 20 per cent forced the CBS, an American firm, to divest its interest to the point where Cascade was required to scurry around looking for purchasers or a partner. We are dealing with people's lives and incomes-real people who live in my riding. I think this is the responsibility of a manufacturing industry to those employees who have employed their skills to build the reputation which the company currently enjoys. What we need right now, with government assistance, is to do these things immediately.
I make four suggestions: First, to apply the 90 per cent export guarantee to Cascade which was requested some years ago. Second, to assist in advancing the financing of foreign sales of Cascade's products through a financing mechanism which I suggested earlier. I am not asking for a loan. Third, a government underwriting, perhaps through a means such as DREE or in some other way, to ensure the ultimate profitability of this company which has great potential. Fourth, that we should consider under

DREE, when you consider the 9 per cent unemployment rate in the lower mainland of B.C., some kind of special spot zoning assistance, especially for those companies outside designated areas and for those companies which have an important technological growth potential, even if they are located outside designated areas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) a question in respect of the regrettable incident which was reported in reference to the visit of Alderman Seguin of Hull to Quebec House in Paris, where the honourable alderman reported he was criticized vehemently by one Mr. Michaud, the cultural aide of the province of Quebec, for wearing a pin which was a replica of the Canadian flag.
The last thing I would like to do would be to exacerbate any tension among peoples in our country, but in my opinion the Secretary of State for External Affairs is the man who is responsible for the well-being and the welfare of Canadians abroad. It is the Secretary of State for External Affairs who issues passports for Canadians abroad and he, and he alone, is responsible for the welfare of Canadians abroad. While he might want to emulate his leader and shrug off a question such as was asked three days ago, I think it is not incumbent upon him, as the pre-eminent and most prominent member of the government in respect of external affairs matters, to shrug off these responsibilities and to say that it is a matter for the Premier of Quebec, or for any other provincial leader, to decide what should be done.
I think it has been clearly demonstrated, as was stated in this House by the illustrious former leader of the government, the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, that in all matters concerning Canadians abroad, in all matters concerning the diplomatic expression of Canada abroad, it is the government of Canada and not the government of any province or any section of the country which must express itself.

June 29, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
In my opinion it is extremely important that when a Canadian is abroad-in this case it is alderman Seguin of Hull-he carries with him the passport of the government of Canada signed by and issued in the name of the Secretary of State for External Affairs who guarantees the good passage and good reception of that particular Canadian abroad. It is totally unbecoming of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, sardonically, absent-mindedly or otherwise, to shrug off his responsibility. I know that he might want to emulate his great leader in terms of shrugging, but it is still the responsibility of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to look after Canadians who are abroad.
I say to you, Sir, and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs-who is not here tonight-that it is the responsibility of that distinguished officer to take note of the rights of Canadians abroad; and the rights of Canadians abroad, guaranteed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, transcend any provincial office whether it be Quebec, whether it be Ontario or whether it be Atlantic Canada. This has been demonstrated. Mr. Pearson mentioned some years ago that the prime responsibility, diplomatically, resides with the government of Canada.
I would like to remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs, had he deigned to be here tonight, that this is his responsibility. He who issues a passport to Canadians abroad should stand behind that passport and guarantee the rights of the Canadian citizen abroad, so that that Canadian citizen be not subjected to the denigrating, humiliating circumstances which, regrettably, was the
case when this very distinguished alderman from Hull visited Quebec House and apparently was told not to wear a Canadian flag replica because that was provocative to one particular province of Canada. This kind of thing is very conducive to disunion in the country.
I think any decent Canadian cabinet minister should assert himself in every way possible to exalt the rights of this dominion, of this country, and-as Mr. Pearson said- should remember that it is the country and not the province which is supreme.
